70m.description: A token that is normally a function word or verb (is, was, were, can, on, will, after, to) sitting in a noun or modifier slot, usually right after a determiner or adjective. Typically it is the first piece of a longer word (werewolf, isomer, wasp, makeshift, afterthought) or is used as a noun ("a can of", "his will").
70m.explanation: Mid-word fragment tokens that start a word split after "a/an/the": a separate token like "were" in werewolf, "is" in isomer/isle, "can" in canes/cancel, "makes" in makeshift, "was" in wasp.

70m.description: Words that start a fixed phrase or template and set up the next slot: 'thank'/'grateful to', 'Due to', 'chose/used to', '#include', '->prepare(', French l', possessive 's, math '/' before the next number.
70m.explanation: Function-word or fragment tokens whose continuation is highly predictable, especially acknowledgement phrases ('thank', 'grateful to', 'indebted to'), sentence-initial 'Due' (to), elisions like l', and word-piece starts across languages.

70m.description: Technical formal contexts: programming code, especially imports/declarations/library names and code Q&A prose, plus math/physics derivation wording ("can be written as", "given by", integral, Eq.).
70m.explanation: Predictable continuation tokens in code imports/boilerplate (React, {, scala, '.', require) and math-paper phrasing like "can [be] derived/evaluated", where the next token is a highly formulaic, expected word.

70m.description: Tokens inside formulaic templates or boilerplate where a slot comes next: sign-off line breaks before names, ** and * in generated math, citation and Category: patterns, footers, stock phrases.
70m.explanation: Predicts structural continuation tokens: the newline after sign-offs/headers ("Thanks,", "Regards,", "Originally Posted by"), the comma after publisher names, and the ** or * operator in polynomial terms of derivative problems.

70m.description: The word completing a fixed or formulaic phrase right after the word that calls for it (represented as, motion for, similar to, recommend that, under various, very much), mostly in formal scientific or legal text.
70m.explanation: Function words/connectors right after a formulaic head word, predicting the standard continuation: 'motion for', 'represented as', 'Thank you very much', 'recommend that', 'something like', 'respectfully dissent', 'according to', 'various'.

70m.description: The token right after a clause's subject (pronoun, relative 'which/who/that', or modal) where the main verb is expected, firing when something other than a plain verb sits there: an adverb, comma, contraction, 'as' or a split verb.
70m.explanation: Token right after a subject pronoun or relative 'which/who' (I, we, they, he, might), where an adverb or parenthetical comma is inserted before the verb (e.g. 'we, as...', 'I really', 'which specifically', 'might as well').

70m.description: Mainly blank lines (⏎⏎) after a finished statement or closing brace inside indented code blocks. Also the joining points in formulaic text: '+/-' between terms in math problems, 'was' in 'study … was conducted', months.
70m.explanation: Blank-line break (double newline) after a completed statement or closing brace inside indented code, before the next statement/method begins; occasionally ' was'/' +' after a subject in prose or math.

70m.description: Inner subword pieces of hard-to-predict strings: words in agglutinative or less-covered Latin-script languages (Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian, Czech) and non-Western names, plus citation-key and legal-reporter number/hyphen parts.
70m.explanation: Mid-word subword fragments inside words in non-English text (Turkish, Hungarian, Finnish, Czech), often a vowel-initial or y-/ğ- continuation after a prefix; also the hyphen in citation IDs like [@B78-viruses-12-.

70m.description: Token beginning the second/final conjunct of a parallel construction: 'or', 'nor', 'but also', 'sino', or the repeated preposition/function word (e.g. 'X for A and Y [for] B') echoing the first conjunct.
70m.explanation: Second-conjunct connectives in parallel/contrastive structures: 'or', 'nor', 'also' (not only...but also), 'another', and especially repeated 'for' in elliptical parallel clauses (X for A and Y for B), anticipating a repeated structure.

70m.description: Fires on the word just before the main verb is expected, most strongly on "to" in "began/started to" and "be" in "yet to/remains to be". Strongest with things or body-part subjects describing a change ("knees began to").
70m.explanation: The infinitive 'to' (or auxiliary/linking verb) right after aspectual verbs like began/started/beginning/yet, predicting an upcoming change-of-state verb (e.g., 'began [to] fray', 'starts [to] brown').

70m.description: Mainly prepositions that start a means/method/manner phrase after a clause ("via" strongest, then "using", "as", "through", "for"). Also the opening of LaTeX display math, labels/refs, and markup/code identifiers.
70m.explanation: Prepositions or connectors introducing a method, means, or reference ("via", "using", "as", "for" in "see X for details"), and also LaTeX display-math openers like "$$\" after a colon or "defined as".

70m.description: Fires on incomplete fragment tokens that need the next token to finish them: split UTF-8 character bytes, tokens ending in a backslash before a LaTeX command or escape (-\, }\, $\), and HTML ><, </.
70m.explanation: Fires on a split multi-byte token: the broken half of a UTF-8 character (mojibake in Turkish/Chinese text) or a backslash-led LaTeX piece (\ , -\, }\) right before a command name like frac, sigma.

70m.description: First token of a name or identifier that starts a new slot: a function argument, list item, statement start or subject. Strongest when the name repeats an earlier variable or entity.
70m.explanation: The first token of an identifier/variable name (e.g. user, root, env, d, db) that repeats a name seen earlier in the context, typically after a comma or at line start in code, predicting its continuation like ->field or _suffix.

70m.description: Joining tokens right before an operand or value in structured text: + - /(- in algebra drills, opening brackets of code function calls, currency symbols or leading digits of money amounts.
70m.explanation: Punctuation/operator tokens that open an argument or operand, mid-expression: open paren after a function/method name in code, ' $' or digits starting a dollar amount, and operators like ' -', '/(-' in algebra exercises.

70m.description: Boundary token after a long unmarked stretch: a new predicate or clause starting without a conjunction (comma lists, run-ons, repeated words) or the extension dot after a long URL, path or identifier.
70m.explanation: Token right after a list of parallel clauses or a long compound predicate, where the next element needs a verb/auxiliary (was, are, have, could) omitted subject; also the period before a file extension in filenames/URLs and at end of math terms.

70m.description: Tokens that continue a clause right after a plural noun phrase, mainly " as" (as described / as well as / classify X as); also plural people/role nouns (mothers, nurses, pessoas).
70m.explanation: The word "as" (or a plural noun like women/mothers/nurses) right after a noun phrase, where it begins an adjunct such as "as well as", "as described", "as a function of", or a role complement.

70m.description: Two related groups: (1) intensifiers and fixed-phrase words in casual speech or prose ('really', 'so', 'as well', 'all right', 'as if', 'were' in 'werewolf'); (2) plural nouns or word pieces inside code identifiers and compound words ('lists', 'types', 'departments', 'providers').
70m.explanation: Adverb/function words after a verb or copula that precede a continuation, like 'really', 'so', 'as', 'all', 'well' (as well, it's really, felt so, all right); also mid-word fragments like 'were'wolf, 'types'.

70m.description: Mixed: author names/initials in scientific citations, power-≤3 terms in 'third derivative' and other math-drill tokens, statistical notation (+/-, N =), curly-apostrophe contractions, and month names after day numbers.
70m.explanation: Mid-word or mid-token continuation points where the next token is highly predictable: the exponent '3' in 'third derivative of ...**3' math problems, author initial periods in citations, name fragments (Kaczmarek), apostrophes in contractions.

70m.description: Adverb (e.g. thereby, thus, often, also, ultimately) sitting in the slot before the verb: right after the subject, or after a clause comma before an -ing phrase. Sentence-initial or post-verb adverbs barely fire.
70m.explanation: Adverbs inserted right after a subject or a comma before a verb phrase, especially "thereby"/"thus" opening a consequence participle clause, also "often", "ultimately", "famously", predicting the upcoming verb or participle.

70m.description: Start of an attached modifier/argument: prepositions 'with'/'in' after verb+object (especially pronoun objects, describing how something was done), and LaTeX sub/superscript markers after operators (\int_, \sum_, \mathbb{C}^, sqrt( ).
70m.explanation: Predicts the continuation after a preposition following a verb phrase of manner/gesture ("looked at him [with] contempt", "nodded [in] salute"), and also LaTeX subscript/superscript tokens after \int, \sum, \mathbb{Z/C}, or sqrt.

70m.description: Two separate jobs: pieces of South Asian (mainly Indian) personal and place names; and sentence-opening connectives ('As shown in FIG.', 'As a result') in patent and scientific writing.
70m.explanation: Mid-word subword tokens inside Indian names (e.g. Utt-arak-hand, Mukhe-kar, Ram-ak-rishna), plus sentence-initial "As" in patent text ("As shown in FIG.", "As a result"), where the next token is predictable.

70m.description: Highly forced continuation tokens inside rigid memorized templates (license text, legal citations/court headers, code idioms, lorem ipsum, constants); also directional 'to' after verb+object marking a destination.
70m.explanation: Predicts the next token in highly memorized boilerplate or formulaic text (legal headers, license text, constants, API calls, citations), firing on mid-phrase tokens like '(', '⏎', ' to', 'Klu[wer]', ' INCIDENT'.

70m.description: Positions where a specific proper name/identifier is expected or in progress: capitalized 'The' before titles/outlets, mid-name fragments, 'v.' case names, '.', '/', ':' before code/URL/caption identifiers.
70m.explanation: Tokens inside a proper-name/title or qualified identifier where a specific continuation is predicted: publication names after 'at/by/in' ("The" Hill), case names (Gaines v. Ski), and separators like context[.], color[:], file[/].

70m.description: Formulaic, highly conventional tokens inside technical or structured documents: license boilerplate, code (especially `return`), scientific-paper markup, section IDs, DOIs and citations, patent and abstract openers, wiki categories, legal headers. Silent on casual or narrative prose.
70m.explanation: Predicts the next token in highly boilerplate/formulaic text: license headers ("you can redistribute", "You may obtain", "FOR ANY"), Go/C `return` statements, and section-number/DOI fragments like {#sec3dot2-...}.

70m.description: Fires on tokens where text moves from a claim to its explanation or evaluation: 'due (to)', 'has the advantage/disadvantage', 'the problem/reason is', 'the case', 'effect', 'e.g.', and colons introducing an explanation.
70m.explanation: Predicts the word right after a noun/copula that introduces an explanation, cause, or pro/con: 'due' (to), 'advantage/disadvantage' (of/that), 'is' (because/that), 'expense', 'case', or a colon introducing the explanation.

70m.description: Tokens that begin or continue a compact value or descriptor in a noun phrase or predicate: decimal points, hyphens, units, abbreviation or name fragments after a/an, phone codes, predicate adjectives ("had been light").
70m.explanation: Fires on the token right after a number/unit or noun where a scientific or technical continuation follows: decimal points in measurements (4.4, 2.5), superscript minus in units (cm^−1), phone-prefix '%', and capitalized abbreviation starts (T2, CPM, DME).

70m.description: Generic or universal statements: the subject or next token after a generic subject (bare plural, generic 'a X', generic 'you/anyone/one/a person') or 'best/important to', typical of legal rules, definitions and advice.
70m.explanation: Token right after a generic subject (noun phrase, 'if', 'a person', 'best') in a general-statement or definition, where a verb/modal like 'is/are/will/to' or pronoun 'you/anyone' is expected next.

70m.description: First token of distinctive names or category terms within a field: famous people, brands, platforms, languages, chemical elements, ideologies/religions, eponymous concepts. Strongest after prepositions or comparisons (under/against/than/of); ordinary names and nouns stay weak.
70m.explanation: A proper name (person, company, element, or concept) that is used as a modifier or is the start of a name, often awaiting a suffix like -ian, -ism, or -Macaulay (Chev|ron, Cohen, Marx, Freud, Cu, Jesus).

70m.description: The main verb slot right after a subject, mostly passive participles or auxiliaries ("is provided/used/applied"). Peaks on judgment verbs (deemed, considered, regarded as, shown to) and when the subject is indefinite.
70m.explanation: Passive-voice participle or verb right after an auxiliary (is/was/are/been), especially 'deemed' and 'considered', also 'provided', 'introduced', 'used', 'required', predicting an evaluative or procedural complement.

70m.description: Connective token (and/or/to/by/after/&/slash/dash/vs/comma) linking two short parallel items in a pair or range, e.g. 'top to bottom', 'side by side', 'July to September', 'hopes and dreams'.
70m.explanation: Connector word (to, and, by, or, &) linking the first item of a paired or ranged phrase, like 'top to bottom', 'side by side', 'July to September', 'hopes and dreams', predicting the second counterpart.

70m.description: Tokens in rigid boilerplate templates (generated math problems, figure/table citation markup, court-opinion formulas, licenses, code); separately, the adverb "first" meaning "before anything else".
70m.explanation: Predicts a highly expected, formulaic next word in boilerplate text: legal phrases (found guilty, the court), 'first' adverbs, 'table'/'fig' ref-types, repeated 'sqrt' in math simplification, and formulaic 'I have hereunto'.

70m.description: Mixed: words opening a clause (esp. 'which' after prepositions, 'and/or that' in legal prose); line breaks after statements in code blocks; characters in random hex/base64/DNA strings; \mathcal{ braces, 'org.', 'Let l('.
70m.explanation: Relative/complementizer words ("that", "which", "what") introducing a subordinate clause after a noun or verb, especially in legal prose; also newlines in code and mid-token pieces of hashes or DNA sequences.

70m.description: Formulaic boilerplate/meta-text around documents: disclaimers, competing-interest/funding statements, copyright/license notices, contact info, URLs, phone numbers, and calls to action (visit/follow/click/for more information).
70m.explanation: Boilerplate web/article endings: contact/"for more information, visit" calls to action, URL domain endings, social follow prompts, and disclaimers/declarations ("authors declare that", "no conflict of interest.", "material is"), predicting the next formulaic phrase.

70m.description: Joining token right after the first part of a multi-part structure: and/or/comma between numbers, math operators, underscores and hyphens in names and ranges. Strongest between numbers in math problems.
70m.explanation: Connector token right after the first item/number in a list or operation (comma, 'and', 'or', '+', '-'), or an underscore/hyphen inside identifiers, where the next token is a second operand or word part.

70m.description: Point in a clause where the main verb is pending: adverbs between subject/auxiliary and verb ('which specifically protects') and unfinished verb-stem subword tokens, especially in Romance languages.
70m.explanation: Fires right after a subject or relative pronoun (we, I, which, who) on an adverb (really, specifically, closely) or on a mid-word verb stem fragment (recon-, constru-, observ-) where a verb continuation is expected.

70m.description: Physical/chemical matter and energy: chemical substances, gases, fluids, electric current/electrons, wind/heat, and protocol conditions like temperatures ("at 37 °C") and buffer compositions in scientific/technical text.
70m.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens in scientific/technical text where a physical quantity, substance, or flow is about to be specified, especially temperatures after "at" (at 37 °C), and words like current flowing, ionizing, argon, CO2.

70m.description: Two unrelated jobs: the verb 'want' (and weakly need/make/wish/seek) after a subject; and tokens inside fixed templates (section-anchor ids, generated maths exercises, legal citation numbers, LaTeX braces, @param).
70m.explanation: Fires on the token after a subject/"if" in "if you/she/I want(s) to" (the verb 'want'), and on structural connectors in section-ID labels ({#sec3dot2-sensors}) or the digit '0' after 'Let c =' in decimals.

70m.description: Tokens continuing a conventional collocation or completing a split word, e.g. news attribution ("told the", "said in"), "didn't", "van den", "hard to", "i =". Strongest after "told" or "said".
70m.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens where the next word is highly predictable, especially "the" after "told" (told the BBC/crowd), "den" in "van den Broek", contraction "n't" after did/doesn't, and mid-word fragments.

70m.description: Wording that describes how things are visually shown: figure/table-caption conventions (dashed lines, red arrows, mean ± SD, asterisks indicate, shown as, sectional view), plus colours/appearance in prose or styling code.
70m.explanation: Figure-legend and table-caption boilerplate in scientific papers: the word right after 'shown/represented/indicated' or a visual descriptor (solid, dotted, red, Color, asterisks, ±, 'as', 'by') that precedes a description of plot styling or statistics.

70m.description: Spots where the next token is easy to predict: first pieces of split French/Spanish verbs (' all'-ons, ' a'-vez, ' n'', ' ten'-emos), and English formula slots ('nothing to', ranges 'X to Y', 'record before', 'No. 10', '#Fig').
70m.explanation: Short function-word or word-fragment tokens just before the rest of a word/phrase, especially French split tokens (to|i, all|ons, a|vez, n|'), plus 'nothing/more to', 'before' (court), and case-number digits.

70m.description: First token of new content right after an opener: indentation/newline starting a code bracket or list (import (, array(, {), and clause-starting 'what'/'that'/'who' after So/But/Now/all; also 'is the'.
70m.explanation: Sentence-initial 'what' (or 'that'/'who') after conjunctions like So/But/Then/Now starting a rhetorical question, plus indentation/whitespace tokens right after an opening bracket or paren in code lists/imports.

70m.description: Fires on plural-looking or bare-verb forms where the context points to a singular, e.g. 'article contain', 'owner conduct(s)', 'only were(wolf)', 'What the hell are'. Weaker on 'all', 'some', 'those' and plural nouns in code.
70m.explanation: Predicts a verb/word continuation right after a subject or wh-word, especially "are" in "What the hell are...", and mid-word verb stems (assess-es, conduct-s, were-wolf) where a suffix or following word is expected.

70m.description: Prepositions (mainly 'between', also 'entre', 'into', 'to', 'from') introducing compared groups or ranges after words of difference, variation, change or group assignment, especially in scientific statistics.
70m.explanation: The preposition "between" (or French "entre") right after words like difference, differ, vary, or significant, introducing the compared groups; also "into"/"to" after randomized/assigned into groups.

70m.description: Two unrelated facets: (1) in code, '=' after typed variable/pointer declarations plus ternary ':', argument commas, '+'; (2) in prose, public sentiment/political faction words (outrage, protests, supporters, right-wing, opposition).
70m.explanation: Tokens right before an expected object/continuation: the '=' after a declared variable in C/ObjC/Java code (pointer type declarations), ternary ':' and casts, plus news words like protests/outrage/supporters/crowd that take a following 'of/against/at' phrase.

70m.description: Mainly negation words (not, n't, never, no, cannot), strongest after contrast or a disappointed expectation (but, however, unfortunately) and in error messages. Separately: opening parentheses and operators in nested arithmetic.
70m.explanation: Negation words right after an auxiliary or verb (n't, not, no, never), predicting the negated verb or predicate to follow; also weakly opening parentheses in nested arithmetic expressions.

70m.description: Sentence-ending periods mid-paragraph in running prose, especially casual opinion or forum posts, where more text follows. Weaker scattered firing on mid-sentence words and verbs in technical text.
70m.explanation: Sentence-ending periods (mostly in informal forum or opinion prose) that complete a declarative statement, just before a new sentence or paragraph begins; also fires weakly on mid-clause function words such as 'is', 'are', and 't.

70m.description: Polysemantic: split-off word prefixes (' re', 'post', 'pre'); punctuation slots in templated math/letter-dict data; 'Q:' newline; RSS 2.0 footer; 'of'/'and' in fixed phrases.
70m.explanation: Tokens where a following word piece is strongly predicted: the " re" prefix (redefine, rewire), "of/from" after nouns, colons in letter-count sets, periods after equations in math problems, and "2." in RSS 2.0.

70m.description: Predictable tokens inside formulaic language of formal/technical documents: licence headers, court-opinion boilerplate, paper declarations/methods, code docs; strongest mid-phrase in stock legal/licence templates. Casual prose near zero.
70m.explanation: Predicts the next word in memorized boilerplate legal/license text (Apache/BSD licenses, court opinion formulas, funding disclaimers), firing on function words or fixed-phrase tokens like 'Apache', 'permitted', 'in', 'to', and possessive 's'.

70m.description: Token right after a word that leaves the clause unfinished, especially necessity/obligation/modal words (requires/imperative/need/must/can): complementizer 'that/to/for/with', or an interrupting dash/comma.
70m.explanation: Function tokens that open a clause or parenthetical after a noun/verb: dashes (– — -) setting off appositives or asides, and "that"/"for"/"with" after requires/need/imperative; also French "laiss-" fragments.

70m.description: Start of a complement after a framing word: the word right after spatial prepositions, mainly 'on' ('on the', 'on the same/other'), and the opening bracket of math expressions ('Let x be (', 'remainder when (').
70m.explanation: Token right after "on the" in contrast/location idioms ("on the [same/other] hand", "On the other hand"), and the opening parenthesis after "Let x be" in synthetic math problems.

70m.description: Technical/problem-solving prose: software, OS and tool names with version numbers (Ubuntu 18.04, SPSS 22.0 (, Python 3.5.1), plus words about practicality, need, advantages, cost or recommendations in technical/patent/scientific text.
70m.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens in technical/patent/StackOverflow text where a specific continuation is expected: software version numbers (Ubuntu 14.04, 10.3), '(' after software names, and 'practical', 'need for', 'recommend', 'advantages of'.

70m.description: Degree, extent or quantity expressions. Fires most on the adjective or adverb right after exclamative or embedded "how" ("how important"). Also fires on "than", "enough", "as far as", "ample" and "thousands of".
70m.explanation: Adjective/adverb or quantity word inside a degree or comparison construction, especially after "how" (how important), plus "than", "as" (as far as), "enough", "ample", predicting the following complement clause.

70m.description: Tokens in the middle of a predictable multi-token unit. Strongest on interior pieces of split words (to|lu|ene, Is|let, Flow|Jo); also on code syntax (., then, {) and fixed pairs (or, and, than).
70m.explanation: Tokens in the middle of a construct where a specific continuation is highly predictable: code syntax (':', '.', 'then', 'throw'), mid-word fragments of multi-token words (aspen, toluene, benzo, olefin), and conjunctions like 'and/or' joining paired adjectives.

70m.description: The word straight after a verb that completes it: object pronouns or nouns, manner/time adverbs (badly, overnight, separately), particles. Prepositions, and adverbs with no verb before them, stay weak.
70m.explanation: Token right after a transitive/action verb that is completing the verb phrase: object pronouns (me, him, us, themselves, it) or adverbs (badly, heavily, intensively, overnight, lightly, once), often just before a prepositional phrase.

70m.description: Mostly fires on causative/phrasal verbs like 'let', 'put', 'keep' and 'make', strongest after 'to', 'and' or a subject. It also fires on mid-word fragments of names and foreign words (Le|h|rich, B|let|chley, 've' of veux).
70m.explanation: The verb "let" (also make, put, keep) right after "to"/"and"/subject, predicting a pronoun object next (let her/him/me go). Weaker on mid-word fragments in names and foreign text.

70m.description: Token starting a new constituent right after an unpunctuated noun phrase, strongest for pronoun-like tokens (I, me, he, she, we), including pronoun-shaped word pieces in noun positions.
70m.explanation: Tokens like "I", "he", "we", "me", "she", "it" (and "guidelines") that start a new clause or are word-fragments, e.g. "I" in IPC/ILEC/IHT, "me" in "mexpp", "she" in "sheaves"; often a pronoun beginning a relative clause.

70m.description: Final pieces of proper names, mostly people's surnames and company or legal-case party names (strongest for rare, multi-token ones), plus the token right after (comma, "v.", "Co.", "Inc.", "'s").
70m.explanation: Final token of a proper name (surname piece, or company/party name in legal case citations), where the name ends and a delimiter like comma, period, "v.", or title/affiliation follows.

70m.description: Non-final fragment tokens inside long multi-token strings: URL/DOI/version pieces (LICENSE-2.0), CLI flags, phone/hex/format codes, and subword pieces of split non-English (Portuguese/Spanish/Czech) words.
70m.explanation: Mid-token fragments inside URLs, phone numbers, version strings, and command-line flags, especially the "2" in LICENSE-2.0 and RSS 2.0, plus numeric URL pieces, hyphen flags, and word-stem pieces in non-English text.

70m.description: Several unrelated patterns: blank line after a closing brace or return in code; helper verb do/did/does in questions or before 'not'; 'of' after part/rest/half/fraction; table dash rules, %, LaTeX '$$'.
70m.explanation: Fires at structural boundary tokens where a predictable continuation follows: blank-line gaps after closing braces in code, table separator dashes, and auxiliary 'do/does/did' or 'of' (part of, third of) in prose.

70m.description: The first content word, usually an adjective or head noun, of a verb's object or complement that gives the subject a quality. Strongest after have/possess/play/issue + a (e.g. "has a remarkable", "plays an important").
70m.explanation: Word right after "play(s) a/an", "had a/an", "have an" etc., where an adjective or modifier is expected (important, crucial, severe, easy), plus mid-word continuations and adverbs like "exponentially".

70m.description: Final token of a modifier before a noun (end of a compound adjective, or the closing bracket/quote of a modifier), strongest in comma-separated adjective lists.
70m.explanation: The final token completing a hyphenated compound modifier inside a descriptive adjective list (e.g. "wood-panelled", "middle-aged", "state-of-the-art"), or the closing parenthesis of a parenthetical adjective, just before the noun.

70m.description: Tokens inside formulaic spans whose continuation is nearly fixed: code 'else', figure/table/page numbers and legal citation parts (L.Ed., Pat. No., *page markers), subtitle timestamps, and mid-word fragments of non-English/rare words.
70m.explanation: Mid-structure tokens in predictable formatted text: the 'else' after a closing brace in code, figure/table reference numbers, star-page markers (*123) in legal text, and mid-word fragments in names or words.

70m.description: A mix of unrelated triggers: number pieces inside codes (postcodes like W1, map grid refs, road numbers, phone codes, opening hours, math constants); "Dis"/"Ex" at the start of split words; physical-action verbs and "to"/"as" in fiction (open, close, take); and "](#" in figure links.
70m.explanation: Mid-word or function-word tokens that predict a specific continuation: word-start fragments like 'Dis'/'Ex'/'El', London postcode digits 'W1', map grid refs, 'close/closed/open', and infinitive 'to' after a subject.

70m.description: Polysemantic unit with several unrelated triggers: non-English text (Albanian, Danish, French 'dit', Spanish 'Señor' in parliamentary addresses), 'based/basis', descriptions of hair and clothing, 'Hey' post openers, and travel-guide listings.
70m.explanation: Mid-word or mid-phrase tokens where a specific continuation is highly predictable: speech tags like "dit" after a quote, "Señor/Hr." before "Presidente/formand", "-based", and adjectives/prepositions awaiting a noun. Multilingual.

70m.description: The determiner right after 'at' (this/that/the/one/some) in phrases giving a time or place, e.g. 'At that point'. Strongest for time uses; weak when 'at' follows a verb ('looked at that').
70m.explanation: The demonstrative or determiner ("that", "this", "the", "one") right after the preposition "at", especially in time phrases like "at that moment/point/time" at sentence start, and also locations like "at the University".

70m.description: Predictable linking word that completes a stock opening phrase just before its object, e.g. 'invention relates', 'Pat. No. X issued', 'definition of', 'point was to', 'as with'. Strongest in formal text.
70m.explanation: Predicts the next word after formulaic head nouns/verbs in patent and academic boilerplate, e.g. "The present invention [relates]", "patent No. X [issued]", "definition/construction/description [of]", "point was [to]", "remanded".

70m.description: The expected token that completes a fixed phrase or template: time words after numbers ("two weeks"), idiom prepositions ("butterflies in"), math-problem templates ("factor of", "for g"), court-opinion paragraph breaks.
70m.explanation: Tokens right after a time-span quantity (two weeks, several hours, ten years) predicting 'ago/later/old'; also paragraph-break newlines before numbered sections in legal opinions, and function words (of, in, for) in math/prose.

70m.description: Tokens filling an expected slot in formulaic, structured text: legal rulings and citations (denied, dismissed, S.Ct), opening hours, prices, clock times, phone numbers, time spans after numbers, polynomial exponents.
70m.explanation: Predictable continuation tokens in formulaic text: legal dispositions (cert. denied, dismissed, reversed, S.Ct.), guidebook price/hours ranges (£x.50, 10am-), phone prefixes (800), and duration words (a year, five months).

70m.description: Fires on the expected next token in fixed formats: patent wording ("directed to", "provides"), patent/ID digits, '.com', citation numbers, '?' after number sequences, "types" after a number, word endings.
70m.explanation: Predicts a continuation in patent/academic boilerplate: the word after phrases like 'directed', 'object of the invention', 'various/different/two/other' ("types"), 'there is' ("provided"), plus patent-number digit fragments and citation endings.

70m.description: Function words at the start of a clause or introductory phrase, before the main content: existential 'there', and the second word of openers like 'On the', 'Just for/to', 'As with', 'compared to', ', like', 'Suppose/Let'.
70m.explanation: Function word right after an introductory adverbial or discourse opener ("On the", "Just for", "As with", "compared to", "Then there", "for every x there"), predicting the clause's continuation like "there is/exists" or a comparison.

70m.description: Polysemantic: do/does/did as auxiliaries (questions, 'did not'); 'of' after part/half/rest/fraction; the last digit or '%' in statistics; the first dash run of a table rule; 'No.' in case captions; 'F.3d'.
70m.explanation: Function words that follow a subject or opener and precede a predicate, especially auxiliary 'do/did/does' in questions or negations, 'of' after 'part/half', plus table divider dashes, percent signs, and 'No.' case numbers.

70m.description: Near-deterministic connector token that completes a formulaic construction just before an open slot: 'have' after could/would, '@' before handles, '=' in URLs, 'dot'/'eq:' in anchors and labels, 'supported by'.
70m.explanation: Fires on "have" after modal verbs (could/would have + participle) in counterfactual constructions, plus structural glue tokens like "dot" in section IDs (sec2dot1), "=" or ":" in URLs/LaTeX labels, and "@" before Twitter handles.

70m.description: Predictable word that completes a common phrase in descriptive or factual prose: places and countries ("Tokyo, Japan", "the world's", town/coast/door), passive verbs (made/used/built/served), and line breaks ending travel-guide listings.
70m.explanation: Predicts a highly formulaic next word in guidebook/lab-methods prose: after "the [world]", "was [used/made/built]", city-comma-[Country] in supplier citations, paragraph-ending newlines, "By the [way]". Fires on tokens preceding stock continuations.

70m.description: Fires where the next token is nearly fixed: strongest on 'or'/'and' right after whether/either/if/with ('whether or not', 'if and only'); also 'wide/entire/whole' and code/figure layout tokens.
70m.explanation: Tokens in the middle of a predictable pairing or repetition, where the next token completes a learned pattern: 'whether [or] not', 'either [or] both', 'spent his [whole/entire] life', 'a [wide] range', and repeated arguments in code or figure caption line breaks.

70m.description: Highly predictable continuation tokens: casual/narrative pronoun-verb tokens ("It"/"it was", "There are", "figured it", "thank you") and second subword pieces of brand/loan words (gour-met, Ge-Force, GoFund-Me).
70m.explanation: Sentence-initial or post-verb pronoun "It" (esp. after "figured"/"figure"), plus "thank [you]", "There [are/was]", and word fragments like "gour[met]", where the next token is a predictable continuation.

70m.description: Tokens partway through a fixed multi-token sequence where the next token is nearly certain: idiom/name linking words (side BY side, Winnie THE Pooh), mid-word pieces, split Chinese characters, boilerplate and formula operators.
70m.explanation: Predicts a highly determined next token mid-pattern: binary minus/plus operators in algebra problems, fixed idioms (spoilt for choice, without specific prior permission, Pliny the Elder), and split multi-byte Chinese/Japanese characters.

70m.description: Word right before a new item is introduced: 'there are/is/'s (also)/will be', 'include(s)/including', 'you'll also find', 'such as', 'among X are', evidence verbs + 'by' ('shown by').
70m.explanation: Verb or particle right after an existential 'there' or in list-introducing phrases ('there are/is also/will be/have been', 'others include', 'as shown by'), predicting an enumerated or additional item to follow.

70m.description: Opening or inner token of a set multi-token name, citation or idiom whose next token is near-certain (San→Diego, Kan.→page number, 'in the face'→of, 'as a matter'→of).
70m.explanation: Abbreviation period after a reporter/state name in legal citations (Kan., Ala., Ga., Cal.), plus the first token of a multi-token proper name (San Diego, Air Force, Jet Propulsion, Qualcomm) in an organization or location.

70m.description: Expected words in formulaic genre text, e.g. Q&A "I want to", lab "for 30 min", recipe "in a medium bowl, whisk", math "Let v(z) be the derivative of", set phrases ("all over the world").
70m.explanation: Predicts a continuation after a subject/preposition where a verb complement or duration follows: mainly "want" in "I want to" (also German/Swedish modals like vill/ten), and duration numbers after "for" (30 min).

70m.description: Points that open an unfinished unit: first or middle fragments of rare, split words and names (often at line start or after dialogue), and clause-opening connectives like if, though, although, because, but.
70m.explanation: Word-start fragments of proper names/capitalized tokens after a line break, quote, or category label (e.g. "Category:Ch"), plus mid-sentence conjunctions like "if", "as if", "though", "although", "because" introducing a clause.

70m.description: Token right after a completed noun phrase: causal verbs (makes/made/leading/led/causes) after an abstract cause phrase, and the newline ending a section-heading phrase or short answer line.
70m.explanation: Newline token right after a short section heading (before a markdown ---/=== underline) or after a Q&A answer line; also causative verbs like 'made/leading' after a noun subject.

70m.description: Connector tokens in formulaic or technical text: "/" in math fractions and pairs like adult/child, "to" in hour ranges, To:, toX code and infinitives, demonstrative "this"/"to". Weak in plain narrative.
70m.explanation: Small connector tokens mid-pattern: the '/' in fractions within math exercises, ' to' in opening-hours ranges ('Mon-Thu, to 11pm Fri'), ' to'/' this' as object or function words, and ':' in timestamps.

70m.description: Tokens that open a span: opening quotes before quoted phrases/strings or dialogue, and code delimiters starting a block. Also nouns pointing to a complement (departure, contribution, transition from, restriction, relation).
70m.explanation: Punctuation/subword tokens right after an opening context where text is structured: opening quotes or brackets in code/dialogue, and words like 'departure', 'contributor', 'LIMITED' (BUT NOT LIMITED), predicting the next continuation.

70m.description: Fires on the token that fills the slot just after a verb or modal: adverbs (just, easily, twice, also), particles (up, out, down), 'or' in 'whether or', and idiom completions (in what way, in turn). It also fires on mid-word pieces in non-English text.
70m.explanation: Mid-phrase word after a verb/modal/idiom where a particle or adverb completes it (could [just], think [twice], in [turn], in what [way], live [up], whether [or]); also partial-word tokens in non-English text.

70m.description: Token linking a defined term/symbol to its definition: separator or verb (',', ':', '=', 'denotes', 'is the', 'means', 'be') in abbreviation glossaries, variable lists, parameter docs; stronger for later list entries.
70m.explanation: The token right after a defined symbol or abbreviation, where its definition is about to begin: a separator (comma, colon, =) in abbreviation lists, or a verb/article like 'is the', 'denotes' after a variable in 'where X is…'.

70m.description: Where the main predicate or a formulaic continuation is about to start in context-dependent formal text: results verbs, framing-phrase commas, '*' in Suppose problems, P<, legal quotation breaks.
70m.explanation: Predicts the next token after a function-like connective in formulaic text: the multiplication '*' in synthetic algebra problems (e.g. 'Suppose 4*x'), '<' in p-values, and verbs like 'agree/confirm/provide' after 'These results'.

70m.description: Function words opening fixed constructions: mainly lowercase 'for' starting a loop or iteration (code, 'Solve … for x', 'for all'), and 'of' after a comma, especially 'of course'; sometimes 'with'/'case'.
70m.explanation: The word "for" starting a loop statement at the beginning of a code line (also "for" ending "Solve ... for x"), and "of" in the phrase "of course" after a comma or sentence start.

70m.description: Unrelated patterns. Strongest is rapid subtitle-style dialogue: the opening quote of the next turn, fillers (uh, oh, yeah) and the commas after them. Weaker: word-initial prefixes (re-, post-, pre-) and 'of' after abstract nouns.
70m.explanation: Fires on a token right after which a continuation is highly constrained: the 're' prefix before a verb stem (rethink, redefine), dialogue-turn closing quotes, 'Uh' in 'uh-huh/uh-oh', and function words 'of/from' or commas in transcript-like text.

70m.description: Token right after a reference to a person (participants, you, those who, someone's), e.g. 'to', 'for', 'by', a possessive apostrophe or 'need', continuing what the person does or is asked to do.
70m.explanation: Function word right after a person/object noun or verb that predicts an upcoming infinitive or complement: 'to' after asked/forced/urge + person, 'need' after subject, possessive ’ before s, 'for'/'by' after ask/passers.

70m.description: Structural word right after a finished subject or phrase, signalling a predictable continuation: auxiliary or verb after a subject ('you'll', 'there's', 'must'), SQL 'FROM', '95%' before CI, 'all', ellipses. Stronger after a preceding clause.
70m.explanation: Function-word token right after a subject or phrase where a predictable continuation follows: contractions "you'll"/"there's", modals ("must", "will"), "%" in "95% CI", and SQL "FROM" after "SELECT *".

70m.description: Verb/predicate token (is, can, would, to, verb suffixes) right after a subject, strongest when the subject is a problem or difficulty ("The problem is"), as in help-request posts and tense narration.
70m.explanation: Predicts the verb/copula or continuation right after a subject noun like "The problem" or "The issue" (mostly "is"), plus similar mid-clause function words ("to", "would"), and question-ending newlines before "A:".

70m.description: Joins one element of a list, pair or expression to the next: list commas, binary operators, connectors in fixed pairs ("X to/for/of Y"), or a repeated word starting the next item.
70m.explanation: Separator or connector tokens within a list or parallel pattern (commas, 'one', 'to', '-', '+', 'for') where the next item repeats the structure of earlier items, as in enumerations, ranges like '30 for 30', and operators.

70m.description: Fires mid-way through formulaic sequences: periods in legal reporter citations (L.Ed., S.W.), slashes in polynomial fractions, time-span/money phrases ("for the past decade", "30-year", "billions of dollars", "$5M in"), and hex/UUID strings.
70m.explanation: Mid-token punctuation in rigid formulaic strings: the period in "L.Ed.2d" legal citations (strongest), the slash in polynomial fractions like "n**7/6300", plus occasional mid-phrase tokens like "year", "for", "dollars".

70m.description: Polysemantic: mainly negation after contrast ('but … not/never/don't'), plus imperative 'press', word-initial ' mar'/' C', nested math parentheses, Chinese characters in code comments, 'sure to'.
70m.explanation: Predicts a verb/adverb right after a clause boundary or subject: imperative "press", negations ("not", "never", "don't"), contrastive "but", plus fragments of split tokens and nested parentheses in math expressions.

70m.description: Tokens inside an unfinished multi-token unit: word fragments in split-up words (strongest in Spanish/French/Portuguese), and the second word of English set phrases like 'if not', 'at no', 'by far'.
70m.explanation: Mid-word subword fragments in Spanish/French/Portuguese words (and 'at'/'if' + 'no/not' constructions) where the next token is a predictable word completion; e.g. 'tí-p-ica', 'jusqu-'-à', 'if not', 'at no'.

70m.description: Mainly fires on later pieces of multi-token South Asian, Middle Eastern or Chinese proper names (Oman, Riyadh, Kolkata). Also fires on the noun 'role' and on the first piece of split words (def-, ex-, dep-).
70m.explanation: Mid-word subword tokens of multi-token place names (Riyadh, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Oman, Shanxi, Uttarakhand) and prefixes like def-/ex-/dep-, plus the noun "role" after a possessive or article.

70m.description: Tokens that open a pending continuation: operand-opening brackets/minus signs and answer starts in templated arithmetic problems, and prose degree/comparative/wh words, especially 'not so', 'too', 'than', 'know where'.
70m.explanation: In synthetic math problems, fires on operator tokens that begin a new term or factor (leading minus after newline, " (-", "*(", "/("). Also on "so" after "not" ("not so often/much").

70m.description: Fires on whitespace padding between table columns, on adverbial/predicative comparative 'more' (also too/much) after be-verbs ('was more careful'), and on hyphens joining compound words.
70m.explanation: Whitespace padding runs between columns in markdown/plain-text tables (column gaps), plus the word "more" after a form of "be" (comparative, e.g. "was more pleased"), and similar words like "Stay" or "attention" in prose.

70m.description: Function words and set phrases inside formulaic, templated text: "What is the" in generated math problems, legal clichés ("reviewed the record", "the facts"), licence and code boilerplate, citation markup. Usually right before the key reference.
70m.explanation: Function words (esp. "the" after "What is/are") predicting the next noun in synthetic math-problem questions; also "the" or "facts/record" in legal opinions, and "=\"@" in Android XML.

70m.description: Fires on object creation and inheritance keywords in code ('= new', 'throw new', 'extends', 'implements'), on a character's body movement or posture in stories ('trudged', 'flopped on', 'onto'), and on comparative 'than'.
70m.explanation: Tokens right after a subject/assignment that predict a following complement: " new" after "var =" in object instantiation code, and motion/posture verbs or prepositions (striding, scurrying, lay on, flopped on, more than) in narrative.

410m.description: Word or word-piece inside a set noun phrase (named term, boilerplate, compound modifier) that leaves it unfinished: compound-modifier endings, stock-phrase determiners ('all the', 'the last'), split-word pieces before the head.
410m.explanation: Mid-word subword fragments (suffix/continuation pieces like -ating, -osing, -ICE) in compound or multi-token words, plus function words like "last"/"the" in "the last", "all the better", where the next token is predictable.

410m.description: Tokens inside an unfinished noun phrase that link to a following nominal: subject-NP coordinating 'and'/'&', figure-panel 'and'/'--', citation parts, and apostrophe-less possessives ('dads house'); also math '**'.
410m.explanation: Tokens in the middle of a compound or list where a word was truncated or the apostrophe dropped: possessive nouns missing their apostrophe (players, Marks, dads), and connectors like 'and' or '--' linking figure panels (A and B, A--G).

410m.description: Token at the end of a sentence-initial or fronted element, just before the clause's subject: the verb after existential 'there', the comma after a fronted prepositional phrase or adverbial, or an inverted verb.
410m.explanation: Predicts the upcoming verb/clause after an introductory element: mainly the "is" in existential "There is" (also was/comes), and commas ending fronted adverbial or prepositional phrases before the main subject.

410m.description: Words that point back to something already mentioned (this/these/such/that/said/same), usually after a preposition in technical or legal prose; weaker on code name pieces repeated from earlier.
410m.explanation: Demonstrative/anaphoric determiners ("this", "that", "such", "these") right after a preposition or verb, referring back to an earlier noun; also mid-identifier tokens (underscores, dots) in code like F_TX_CLOSE macros.

410m.description: Mainly the comma, 'and' or 'or' before the next or final item in formal lists of abstract nouns, verbs or adjectives. More weakly: fixed formulas ('Originally Posted by', 'once in a while') and breaks between forum comments.
410m.explanation: Connective tokens in lists or boilerplate phrases ("and", "or", commas before the final item, "of", "by") and paragraph-break newlines, where the next word is a predictable continuation of a list or formulaic phrase.

410m.description: Text that criticizes, warns about or objects to something harmful (flaws, prohibitions, bad consequences, errors). It fires most on the words that carry on the complaint, like 'and', 'to', 'by allowing', 'would encourage'.
410m.explanation: Predicts a continuation after a negated or disapproved clause, firing on the word right after a negation or prohibition (not, stop, don't, refuse) or on a conjunction/verb where a negative outcome or verb phrase follows.

410m.description: Predictable tokens inside formulaic, specialist text: legal citations (Tex.Civ.App., Fed. R.), list/section markers, abstract-opening "To", known code identifiers, author-name lists. Near zero on ordinary prose.
410m.explanation: Short structural tokens in formal citations and outlines: list/section markers (a, b, 1, d, iii), legal reporter fragments (App, Civ), name-part or identifier joins (commas, underscores), and abstract-opening "To" after a title.

410m.description: Mainly the verb right after a newly introduced agent who arrives or approaches (came, approached, burst, wander). Also fires on word-final pieces like '-ic' in acids/names, and on score hyphens.
410m.explanation: Fires on the token right after a subject noun (often a person/creature) at a verb or particle of approach/arrival (came, approaches, enters, show up), and on mid-word chemical/name fragments like -ic in acids.

410m.description: Parallel/repeated structure: commas and conjunct openers within noun-phrase lists/coordinations ("Neither the", "A, B, and"), plus re-mentioned names/phrases and repeated variables in math/code.
410m.explanation: Predicts a repeated or parallel item in a coordinated structure: commas after list items before 'and', 'the' after 'Both/neither', and repeated tokens in math expressions or LaTeX, anticipating the next parallel element.

410m.description: Words that open a complement or argument: prepositions after verbs (start by, equal to, in [@cite]), "more than" before a number, transitive verbs after modals. Also some word pieces inside chemical names.
410m.explanation: Function words/prepositions right after a verb or phrase that predicts a specific continuation, like 'start [by]', 'equivalent [to]', 'more [than]', 'by [reducing]'; also the space before citation/reference markers ([@...], \[sec:...]) and mid-word fragments.

410m.description: Mainly 'of' (or 's) right after a quantity/container noun (cup of, loaf of, volumes of, night's); also tokens repeating an earlier parallel pattern (repeated code calls, indices, 'yeah, yeah').
410m.explanation: Predicts a repeated or copied token in a pattern: mainly "of" after container/quantity nouns (cup, pound, volume, rack of), also "'s" in "night's", and repeated identifiers or method names in code/LaTeX.

410m.description: Words inside a phrase naming an unspecified item someone will choose, supply or quantify over: instructions, 'any/each/the X you want', conditionals, placeholders and variables. Specific past events stay silent.
410m.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens (often pronouns like 'you'/'your', determiners, or a noun) inside instructional or descriptive clauses where a verb or object must follow, e.g. 'the command you [want]', 'a site you [like]', 'near [your] location'.

410m.description: Word-piece tokens ending in 'r' (mostly 'or', e.g. Sor, wor, tor, cor, hor, ur) at the start or middle of a word split into several tokens; whole words barely fire.
410m.explanation: Word-fragment tokens in the middle of a word that start with 'or'/'sor'/'tor'/'cor'/'wor' (e.g., Sorbonne, Worcester, torque, corroborated, Toronto), predicting the continuation of the word.

410m.description: Media/communication channel words (Twitter, Facebook, online, internet, radio, TV, email, phone, social media); separately, interior tokens of fixed multi-token names/identifiers (Ministry of, hors d', request_mem_region) and commas between equations.
410m.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens in compound or list constructs, especially web/social words (online, Twitter, social media, radio, email) after 'on/a/my', plus mid-word fragments and list commas in code, math and legal text.

410m.description: Positions where a new variable/parameter/symbol name is introduced or expected next: lambda/function params, 'as' bindings, closure '|', 'Let x', math '$v$' and algebra variable slots.
410m.explanation: Token right after a keyword that introduces a new binding or parameter list, where a name or delimiter is expected next: 'Let [x]' in math problems, '|' in block params, '(' after #define macro or function, 'as' in with/except.

410m.description: Modifier/descriptor tokens inside a definite or specific noun phrase before its head appears (the + adjective, possessive 's, title before a name, X-based/X-specific); weak after 'a' or in predicate position.
410m.explanation: Modifier or possessive token inside a noun phrase (adjective, hyphenated compound part, or 's) where the head noun is expected next, e.g. 'nearby', 'handy', 'Gram-negative', 'Backbone's'.

410m.description: Polysemantic: chemical name fragments after locant hyphens (2-[ethyl], 3-[methyl]); operators in a second linear equation; code '{⏎\t' indents; rare-name subwords (E[ry]ri, J[iao]); collocation heads (full of, covers, talk to, X- or Y-).
410m.explanation: Mid-word fragments inside chemical names or rare proper nouns (e.g. 'ethyl', 'methyl', 'Ery', 'ano'), plus operators (+, -) in algebra problems, and code-block newlines/tabs; predicts the continuation of a split word or expression.

410m.description: Tokens finishing a second item in a parallel, contrast or list that repeats the first item's form, plus closing brackets and quotes at the end of such structures. Diffuse and context-dependent.
410m.explanation: Mid-text positions where the next token is a predictable repetition or continuation of an earlier phrase, such as a repeated term, matching bracket or closing punctuation, in scientific, code and LaTeX text.

410m.description: First content token (head noun or word-initial prefix like sub/over/non) of a noun phrase right after a determiner/preposition, in formal or technical text; also some code/math delimiters.
410m.explanation: Fires on the token right after "the/a/of" in a noun phrase, where a head noun or prefix is expected next (e.g. "course of", "sub-", "set of", "half of"); also on code newlines/parentheses.

410m.description: Mainly two unrelated patterns: 'least' in 'at least' setting a numeric minimum (also 'a minimum of'), and verbs of coming back ('return', 'come back'). Plus scattered noise: chemical subscripts, legal 'remand', dates.
410m.explanation: The word "least" in the phrase "at least" (before a number or quantity), plus related predicted-continuation tokens like "return/returned" and date month names in formulaic records.

410m.description: Predicate after a dummy 'it' (it is common/easy/rare/okay to…, it's raining), and the comma after a short judgement or exclamation in dialogue, before a name or add-on (Nice work, Tom).
410m.explanation: Predicts what follows a short evaluative clause: either the adjective slot in 'it is [common/rare/easy/fair] to/that...' constructions, or the comma before a direct-address name in dialogue ('Nice work, Hawkins').

410m.description: Fires mid-way through bound units: inner pieces of rare split words/names (fled[g]ling, Tra[fal]gar), and for/as/into after passive procedural verbs (used for, stored for later, divided into).
410m.explanation: Mid-word subword fragments inside rare multi-token words/names (Snowdonia, Trafalgar, Congolese, Scuderia), plus predictable function words after passive verbs in methods text (for, into, as) and 'Competing' in 'Competing interests'.

410m.description: Fires on heritage/past words in travel-guide text (former, Roman, ancient, artefacts, relics), on commas/'and' after noun phrases in technical prose, and on periods ending math problems ('for b.').
410m.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens where the next word is a predictable continuation: 'former' in travel-guide descriptions, word-fragment 'arte(facts)', and list commas or the period after 'for x' in math problems.

410m.description: Nouns naming an action or process (gerunds used as nouns like 'pitching', 'writing'; -tion/-sis/-al/-ment nouns), and the 'is/was' plus passive verb right after such a subject. Not progressive verbs.
410m.explanation: Verbal-noun/gerund (-ing, -tion, -ment) tokens naming a process or activity (e.g. computing, editing, dephosphorylation, writing, interviewing), often as the subject noun of a clause, predicting a following verb like 'is'/'was' or a head noun.

410m.description: Tokens closing a predictable unit: strongest on C #endif; also closing tags/figure labels echoing earlier numbers, final pieces of names/words, 'he/she' after quotes, list delimiters.
410m.explanation: Predictable continuation tokens in structured text: 'endif' after '#' in C preprocessor blocks, closing digits of figure/line IDs (f4, fig4), 'he' after a closing quote in news attributions, and word-completion fragments of names/categories.

410m.description: Polysemantic: words about availability or prevalence (available, common, seen, found, rare); legal citation volume numbers before F.2d/U.S.; the dot in Go types (context.Context); pieces mid-name (Vir|at); un- prefixes.
410m.explanation: Predicts a highly predictable continuation token mid-phrase: adjectives after 'be/is' (available, common, found), '.' after Go package names (types., context.), and case-citation reporter volume digits starting with 9 (9xx F.2d).

410m.description: Words inside the reach of a negation or similar word (not, without, no, nor, before…could, none, n't). Strongest in contrasts like 'although it may not', 'even if…not', 'without being X'.
410m.explanation: Token right after a negation or concessive/temporal subordinator (without, not, didn't, even if, although, before he), predicting the continuation of a negated or hypothetical clause, e.g. 'being', 'could', 'not', 'anything'.

410m.description: Punctuation delimiters opening or closing a marked span: emphasis/action asterisks, string-closing quotes before concatenation, comment terminators, em-dash breaking off speech; weaker on emphatic phrases ('all the', 'damn').
410m.explanation: Closing or stray punctuation tokens (asterisks, quotes, em-dashes, apostrophes) at emphasis/quote/comment boundaries, often marking where a span ends or interrupts; also 'the' after 'all' in 'all the way'.

410m.description: Mainly forms of the verb 'take' (took, taken, taking; idioms like take place, take on). Also passive participles (discovered, built), variables in math expressions, and tokens in legal citations or funding names (Framework, Circuit, ed.).
410m.explanation: Fires on a verb/participle (especially "taken/take/taking") right after an auxiliary or subject, where a passive or phrasal verb is expected (taken a turn, take advantage, been discovered). Also fires on math variables and institution names.

410m.description: Linking token right after a term, abbreviation, symbol or foreign word, just before its gloss (means, for, stands for, denotes, '(', ',', '--'). Weaker: middle word of 'X by/after X'.
410m.explanation: Token right after an abbreviation, acronym, or foreign term that introduces its definition or translation: "for", "means", "(", ",", ":", "--" preceding the expansion/gloss (e.g. 'Latin for', 'ACL (', 'SBP,').

410m.description: Greek letter tokens (alpha/α, beta/β, gamma/γ, delta), strongest in chemical and biological names. Weaker on words that start set terms: primary, secondary, self-, X(-ray), United, double, public.
410m.explanation: Greek-letter prefix tokens (α, β, γ, 'alpha', 'beta') in chemical/biological nomenclature, e.g. α-helix, β-glucan, α-fetoprotein, right before a hyphen; also weakly 'primary' and 'self'.

410m.description: Clause-boundary token that ends a fronted introductory phrase, most often the comma after a fronted participial or locative phrase ("Spread across the hills, …"). Also inverted or clause-final verbs ("ha llegado", "zieht sich"); noisy mid-word tokens elsewhere.
410m.explanation: Mid-word subword fragments and function tokens where the next token is a predictable continuation, especially commas ending a fronted descriptive phrase before the main subject (e.g. 'Deep, dark and narrow,' → Loch Ness).

410m.description: Mainly the connecting words in a person's life-history narration (born and raised in, grew up, worked as a, years, moved to). Separately and more weakly, math/LaTeX operators and braces.
410m.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens in biographical statements about a person's background or career (e.g. "born and [raised]", "worked as [a]", "grew [up]", "Mr[.]"), predicting the next detail; also operators/symbols in math expressions.

410m.description: Fires on continuation tokens inside multi-token proper names and identifiers: later subwords or words of brands, institutions, places and websites (Joom|la, St John|'s, Lehigh| Valley, national|trust). Also fires on code variables named after their type (JSRuntime *rt).
410m.explanation: Fires on the middle or final sub-token of a multi-token proper name, brand, or compound (Joomla, WooCommerce, St John's, National Trust, OpenStreetMap), where the next token completes or follows a known named entity.

410m.description: Mid-unit tokens of fixed multi-token sequences, mainly the period after stacked initials before a surname (M.G.C. Resende) and the separator in times (h9.30am); also idiom middles ("as … as", "Jack of All").
410m.explanation: Period after an author's middle/first initial in citations (e.g. "M.G.C.", "J.B.A.") before the surname; also the period in opening hours like "h9.30am". Weaker on comparative "as" and code tokens.

410m.description: Enumeration/numbering structure: list item and reference labels like (a), ii, 1), Fig. 3B, xiii, [12], plus the punctuation/newline right after an announced list ('two reasons:', 'as follows:').
410m.explanation: Enumeration markers introducing list items: the punctuation or newline after 'two reasons/cases/options' announcing a list, and labels like (a), (ii), b, iii, Roman numerals starting a enumerated item or panel.

410m.description: Fires on 'right' (strongest in hand/side/positional senses, e.g. 'right hand', 'right-handed', 'right next to'; 'left' weaker) and on nouns heading fixed phrases: 'as a result', 'on the basis of', 'point of view', 'by means of', 'meaningfully'.
410m.explanation: The word 'right' (also 'point', 'basis', 'result', 'meaning') as the start of a word or phrase, e.g. 'right hand', 'right-hand side', 'right angles', 'on the basis of', 'as a result', 'point of view'.

410m.description: Two unrelated patterns: (1) evaluative or effect phrases judging consequences (harmful, fatal, outcome of, detrimental to), including the following preposition; (2) the 'MAP' link in travel-guide venue listings.
410m.explanation: Mostly the "MAP" token in Lonely Planet-style travel listings ("(MAP GOOGLE MAP") after a place name and category; also weaker on mid-phrase words in scientific or general text (e.g. "in", "mod", "with") where a noun/complement is expected next.

410m.description: Mainly words placing events in time, durations or deadlines ('days later', 'within', 'tomorrow', 'extension of time'); separately, ==/!= comparison operators in code conditionals, plus #include/brace tokens.
410m.explanation: Function words or tokens right after a subject/time noun that predict a specific continuation: time-offset words ("days later", "next day"), comparison/range prepositions (to, from, for), and "==" in code conditions.

410m.description: Mixed: in prose, kin/life-story words (his mother, childhood, grew up), venue nouns (the bar), legal parties and dialogue 'How' and speech verbs; in code, connectors like xsl for-each hyphens, form_for, $this.
410m.explanation: Token right after a word that predicts a fixed completion: 'grew [up]', 'for [Defendant]', 'in the [bar]', 'his [mother]/[childhood]', 'for-[each]', 'form_[for]', French 't[-]il'. Predicts a specific next token.

410m.description: Two unrelated clusters. (1) Drinking/smoking: 'drinking', 'smoking', sipping, pouring, glass/bottle/pint of a drink. (2) Comprehension/awareness: 'understand(s/ood)', grasp, comprehend, 'sense of', awareness, familiar, recognize, listen.
410m.explanation: Verbs of drinking (drinking, sipping, drink) and 'understand/understood', plus 'sense of', 'bottle/glass of', 'fired'; the token right before an expected object or complement, often a beverage or comprehension.

410m.description: Tokens within concrete, specific content, mainly mid-clause in narrated events (verb, particle or article before the object), plus pieces of technical identifiers; near-silent on abstract or generic statements.
410m.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens where the next word is highly constrained by a just-started construction: after verbs/participles (suspended after, picked up, had been), inside split identifiers/words, and sentence-final punctuation in formal text.

410m.description: Single lowercase letter tokens with no space before them: letters inside random strings or hashes, the first letter of a split word, and markers like (a) or (b). Capitals and whole words stay near zero.
410m.explanation: A single lowercase letter token (often d, e, s, v, b, r) in the middle of random alphanumeric strings like hashes, URLs, tweet short links, or IDs, or a word-initial letter after a punctuation mark.

410m.description: Polysemantic: closing quotes ending fiction dialogue lines; word-start fragments (ge/re/e) in Turkish/Hungarian/German; legal boilerplate (SUBSTITUTE, Appellee); sequence numbers in math or tables; code indentation; titles like 'vice'.
410m.explanation: Predicts the next token at a point where a highly predictable continuation follows: closing quote marks ending a dialogue sentence before a paragraph break, or mid-word/boilerplate fragments (e.g., SUBSTITUTE, Appellee, Turkish word pieces).

410m.description: Subject pronoun starting a comparative or reduced relative clause ("than I", "as we", "the best I can"), and numbers or labels naming a preceding noun ("UE 330", "Bus 440").
410m.explanation: Token right after a comparative 'than'/'as' (mostly 'than I'), or a reference numeral/number label (e.g. 'terminal 310', 'Bus 440') — the next item being a short subject pronoun or identifier in technical/numeric text.

410m.description: The tokens "long" and "far" used for length, duration, distance or degree ("long-term", "long history", "long ago", "far more", "far from"). Weaker on other extent/degree words ("short-", "much", "vastly", "full", "out").
410m.explanation: The adverbs/adjectives "long" and "far" (also "Long"/"Far" and the "long" in "longitude"), especially before "-term", "overdue", "run", "list", or "more/from" — extent in time or distance or degree.

410m.description: Words that refer back to an entity: pronouns and demonstratives starting a clause ('those', 'that', 'they'), possessives and owned nouns, reused code/math variables; also decade 's' and indentation after comments.
410m.explanation: Predicts a continuation after a short function-like token: indentation after a newline in code, 's after decades/possessives (1970s), 'those'/'that' after 'For'/'But', and the '/' in license URLs.

410m.description: Diffuse, genre-general unit: fires on mid-construction continuation tokens (operators in math templates, prepositions, conjunctions, verbs, modifiers) in fluent information-dense text; weak on trivial, listy or isolated simple sentences.
410m.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens where a continuation is needed: operators (+, -) in algebra word problems, participles/adjectives (restored, converted), 'weather' in 'if the weather's good', and conjunctions/prepositions inside clauses.

410m.description: Tokens that leave a unit unfinished and force a continuation: line breaks inside incomplete sentences (before equations, lists, page breaks), word-start fragments (Rec-, supp-), split bytes, number+%, open brackets.
410m.explanation: Double-newline/blank-line tokens in scraped documents (legal opinions, LaTeX/markdown text) where a paragraph or block break occurs mid-sentence or before an indented equation/list; also fires on mid-token splits (%, �, *).

410m.description: Joining/prefix tokens inside compound names or numbered labels (hyphens like T-/Al-/X-, -based; repeated list prefixes like CD/STAT; decimal points in number lists), right before the distinguishing segment.
410m.explanation: Mid-word or mid-compound tokens, especially hyphens joining a short capital/prefix to a following word (T-Mobile, D-Wave, Al-Sanadid, 16-bit, X-based), plus split identifiers and numbers where the next piece continues the name.

410m.description: Final token of a descriptor directly before the name it labels: titles/roles/categories before proper names in prose ("forward Zack", "inhibitor JQ-1", "called X"), and type tokens before variable names in code.
410m.explanation: Fires at the end of a type/role noun or declaration type token (e.g. 'staffer', 'chelator', 'List<C>', 'Foo *', 'Ref', 'forward'), right before a proper name or variable name is expected.

410m.description: Degree/extremum words (much, far, less, least, min, minimum, max), especially phrase-initial, plus prefix or middle word pieces in split words (mis-, C-is-platin, ic-osa-hedron, N-ishi).
410m.explanation: Word-start fragments and words beginning with "m/mis/min/much/less/far" (much, min, mis-, Miles, Juda-ism, Nishi, -ensa-, -osa-), especially quantity/degree words like "much", "far", "minimum", and subword pieces of such names.

410m.description: Mainly possessive words (whose, his, her, their, your, its, our, my) and words that open a linking phrase (according, based, depending, due, regardless). Also fires on URL starts (http/https). Stronger with longer context.
410m.explanation: Function words that open a dependent or modifying phrase and predict a following noun or clause: possessives (her, their, your, whose), "According", "depending", "based", "pursuant", and URL scheme starts (http).

410m.description: Mixed bag with no shared pattern: sentence-final periods, commas after 'Yes' in dialogue, final digits of scores and IDs, 'first' after 'But', pronouns or possessives after verbs ('try your', 'believe you').
410m.explanation: Fires on the token right after a common function-word or punctuation slot where the next word is highly predictable, e.g. comma after "Yes", "But first", pronoun after "believe", or possessive "his/your/their" before a noun.

410m.description: Segment boundaries: a colon, dash, question mark or line break after a complete headline or title; hyphens joining verb and pronoun in Romance languages (manter-se); first pieces of rare names (L, Del, Al).
410m.explanation: Punctuation or word-fragment tokens that join or introduce a continuation: colons after headline titles, hyphens before clitics (Portuguese -se, -lá), and mid-word pieces like "Del" or "Con" in names and phrases.

410m.description: First predicate word right after a clause's subject: verb/auxiliary after full noun subjects (strongest in embedded what/whether clauses), or the adjective in extraposed 'it is ADJ to/that'.
410m.explanation: A predicate word or verb right after a subject (esp. "it is/was" or a plural subject) that predicts a following "to"/"that" clause: adjectives like normal, common, rare, fair, easy, or verbs like stop, sit, stand.

410m.description: Words just before a predictable non-human noun phrase: commas after opening descriptive phrases, verbs placed before their subject, and possessives of things ('s, its, their, whose).
410m.explanation: Tokens ending an introductory phrase/noun where a subject noun or main clause must follow: commas after fronted modifiers, possessives ('s, its, their), and verb stems, anticipating the head noun or main subject.

410m.description: Continuation points: word-start subword pieces (ha|rem, h|iccup, Hak|ob), connectives/prepositions after a finished noun phrase or clause (or, before, pour, to), plus formulaic slots like citation 'So.2d' and math '+'.
410m.explanation: Function-like connector tokens mid-sentence after a noun/clause, especially "before", "or", "pour", "+", and the "2" in "So.2d" citations, where the next token continues a phrase or list.

410m.description: Mixed: characters inside hex/random alphanumeric strings; range/linking tokens between numbers or dates (to, –, and, hyphen in '100-mile'); and commas/'and'/'for' interrupting a long unfinished subject before its verb.
410m.explanation: Tokens in mid-phrase positions where a continuation is predicted, like commas after a name/date introducing an appositive or relative clause, and fragments inside random hash/ID strings or repeated letter sequences.

410m.description: The head token of a noun phrase or referential pronoun naming a specific entity, inside a clause. Strongest for 'it' or a noun as the subject after which/where/if/when, and for topical technical nouns (spin-wave, RNA, cytokine).
410m.explanation: Token right after a repeated or previously-mentioned noun/term (spin-wave, MHV RNA, van der Waals, β-cell) or a pronoun/closing quote, where the next word continues a compound or modifies a head noun.

410m.description: Tokens that open an open-ended range of uses, places or examples: 'used for/as', 'such as', 'like', 'including', 'found along/around', 'everything/anyone', 'on [platform]'.
410m.explanation: Words right before an expected list of examples or uses/locations: "used [for/as]", "such [as]", "things [like]", "including", "found [along]", "all sorts [of]", typically in descriptive or encyclopedic text, and also indefinite "someone/anyone" fragments.

410m.description: Mid-phrase tokens with a strongly expected continuation: 'of' after duration or quantity nouns and time-span words; series labels (A/B, 12A, HTTP/1.1); expectation and comparison words (want, expect, the same).
410m.explanation: Predicts a highly constrained next token in fixed collocations or enumerations: the "of" after nouns like "run/period/series of", "the same", "unusual", labels like panel/step "A", and version-number dots like HTTP/1.1.

410m.description: Element/tag names (and attribute names) opening new elements in HTML/XML/XAML markup, and factual physical/clinical descriptions of appearance ("revealed a", colors, shapes, age/sex descriptors).
410m.explanation: Element name right after an opening '<' in HTML/XML markup (mostly div, also p, td, li), predicting the attribute or content that follows; also weaker on medical-report words like 'revealed a/an' and color adjectives.

410m.description: Strongest on verbs of drinking, pouring, smoking or firing in scenes (e.g. 'drinking tea'); also fires on unrelated spots: figure/list numbers, math constants, code newlines, post-dialogue breaks/'as'.
410m.explanation: Predicts a following object/complement after participles or verbs of drinking/consuming/firing (drinking, smoking, bottle of, glass of), plus mid-sentence continuation tokens like 'as', 'more', and paragraph-break newlines after dialogue.

410m.description: Tokens that leave a construction open and expecting its argument: transitive/causative action verbs (sent, put, cut, pour), possessives/determiners right after them, wh-question auxiliaries (what do/does/'s), and identifier joiners (_, quelqu').
410m.explanation: Fires on the word after a verb/"what" where a direct object or complement is expected next: transitive verbs of transfer/cutting (sent, cut, put, set), "what do/does/'s", and possessive 's or underscores.

410m.description: Mainly 'and'/'or' joining wh-words or verbs in set phrases ('how and why', 'if and only if'); also 'those' after 'for', pronoun 'that', maths/code single-letter symbols, word fragments.
410m.explanation: Function/connective words in mid-phrase where a continuation is expected, especially "and" after "how/what/when" ("how and why"), "those" after "For", and "a" in "year and a half"; also some math/LaTeX tokens.

410m.description: First token of a fixed multi-token term, strongest on technical modifiers after a/the ("a molecular"→weight, "the amino"→acid). Also URL/figure-anchor pieces, first name pieces, licence boilerplate.
410m.explanation: Predicts a mid-word or mid-phrase continuation token, especially scientific adjectives like "molecular"/"chemical" before weight/mass/shift, plus word-fragment starts (bi-, mo-, F-) and URL slashes or anchor 'f' tokens.

410m.description: Polysemantic: 'is/was' after a framing noun phrase ('The point is'); lab-measurement adjectives (measured, invariant, distilled, observed); middle pieces of rare names; line breaks in hex-constant tables; 'Like this: Like'.
410m.explanation: Predicts continuation after a statement-introducing word: copula "is/was" after "The point/thought/question", or verbs like "note/mean/measured", followed by a "that" clause. Also fires on newline after hex constant values and mid-name tokens.

410m.description: Words set by earlier context: repeated math variables in polynomial/collect-terms drills, second mentions of names and nouns, pronouns pointing back, and adjectives like original/natural/general/real/official after its/the.
410m.explanation: Predicts a repeated or continuing token: the variable in algebra polynomial strings (e.g. "14*y", "- 37*i"), and mid-phrase words like "real", "natural", "general" or name fragments (OpenSC-AD, Adv-ACT) where the next word is highly constrained.

410m.description: Words that come right before a person's name: authorship "by"/"By", spouse/kin words (husband, wife), titles (CEO, Speaker, head of). Also the inner pieces of multi-token names or words, strongest when that word appeared earlier.
410m.explanation: Authorship attribution "by" after titles/'written by' (also author/name starts), and mid-word fragments of proper names or compounds (Zuckerberg, Mendeleev, Suffolk, SourceForge) where the next token is a predictable continuation.

410m.description: Continuation token completing a multi-token unit: inner/second subword pieces of rare technical words or names, head nouns of set phrases ("dynasty", "inhibitors"), range-end years, and inter-block blank lines.
410m.explanation: Mid-word subword pieces or final tokens completing multi-token technical/taxonomic terms (Gelechiidae, mahogany, typhimurium, inhibitors), plus paragraph/chapter-break blank lines and year endings; predicts a continuation or suffix.

410m.description: Mainly nouns naming a collection, kind or label that expect a following specifier ('a series/pair/class/set/type of', 'strain A59', 'version 6.36'); separately, characters inside hex hash/ID strings.
