410m.explanation: Collective/quantifier nouns after an article or demonstrative that expect "of" next (a [series] of, a [pair] of, this [type]/[class]/[set] of), plus back-references like "above/previous/described" and list or hex-ID fragments.

410m.description: Words about possibility or ability (way, chance, possible, impossible, able, unable, ability, managed, failed), strongest when denied ("there was no way", "no chance"), plus legal exception words like "Unless" and "Provided".
410m.explanation: Word completing a possibility/ability/negation construction, predicting an upcoming infinitive: "no [way]", "little [chance]", "impossible/possible", "unable"; also license-header "Unless" (required by applicable law).

410m.description: Mixes unrelated patterns: mid-word fragments like 'ar'/'val'/'Dar' (decARboxylation, CaernARfon, BismARck); 'When'/'as soon as' opening a clause; and emphasis adjectives after 'the' (real, actual, bigger, true).
410m.explanation: Sentence-initial "When" starting a temporal clause (often after a paragraph break or quote), plus mid-word "ar" fragments (chaparral, Caernarfon, decarboxylase), and adjectives like "real"/"bigger" after "the".

410m.description: Words marking historical past or heritage, e.g. 'former', 'past', 'once', 'has been', 'ancient', 'Roman', 'artefacts', 'relics', 'period', mainly in travel-guide text about old buildings and places.
410m.explanation: Words denoting history, age or former status in travel-guide descriptions of buildings/places ("former", "past", "Roman", "been" as in 'has been converted', 'artefacts', 'Egyptian' cotton), predicting a historical/heritage description to follow.

410m.description: Tokens whose continuation is nearly fixed: word fragments (' trium'→phal/phant, 'AR'→CHER), set collocations ('watch out', 'Earl's', 'importance', 'sum', 'distinguished by'), and the period ending equation systems in math problems.
410m.explanation: Mid-word or mid-phrase tokens where the continuation is highly predictable: periods ending equation sentences in synthetic math problems, 'trium' before phal/virate/phant, 'out' after 'watch', and name fragments like 'AR' in Archer.

410m.description: Mainly digit groups inside structured numbers (phone numbers, docket/statute numbers, figure/section numbers, timestamps, math coefficients); separately, patchy firing on verb/preposition/pronoun words in prose.
410m.explanation: Digit tokens inside structured numeric identifiers, especially the middle of UK phone numbers after the area-code hyphen in travel guides, plus case/section/figure numbers and math terms, where the next piece is predictable.

410m.description: Diffuse, low-specificity unit: fires mid-prose on contextually-dictated 'glue' tokens — prepositions, conjunctions, connectives (into, by, to, in fact) and sub-word/URL/notation continuations; silent on word lists.
410m.explanation: Function words or word fragments (prepositions like by/to/into/of, 'fact', citation-start spaces) where the next token is a predictable continuation, e.g. a verb-ing, citation marker, or mid-word completion in scientific text.

410m.description: Tokens that complete or continue a specific item where context strongly constrains it, mostly in dense structured/reference text: hex tables, page ranges, templated math problems, taxonomy entries, code arrays, set phrases.
410m.explanation: Mid-token continuation inside numbers, hex values, ranges and technical/scientific lists, especially the next digit or fragment of a numeric string (0x4c52, 297449,297578, page ranges 323–366), plus abbreviation/list punctuation.

410m.description: Strongest on news photo captions (dates, places, final period before a credit). Also fires on 'United States'/'U.S.' in legal citations, error messages, and 'old'/'remember'/'you know' in fiction.
410m.explanation: Predicts continuation after a sentence-ending period in photo captions or inside citation names: "United [States] v.", "F.A[.] Paneth", "U.[S]", and "old" before friend; also dates ending captions.

410m.description: Second token of a set unit after a short, vague opener: the word after opening 'For'/'To' ('for THE record', 'For ALL', 'For more INFORMATION') or the piece after a short word fragment (T-shirt, k-UD-os, sh-AB-by, t-UND-ra).
410m.explanation: The token right after the word "For/for" in idiomatic phrases ("for the record", "for all", "for more information", "for completeness"); also fires on word-internal fragments like T-/Sh-ab/ke-b, as in T-shirt, Shabtai, kebabs.

410m.description: Junction tokens in formulaic or structured text where a set continuation follows: closing dialogue quotes before speaker tags, URL/code/table delimiters, tweet attribution dashes, template slots like 'picked without replacement from'.
410m.explanation: Predicts a repeated or structurally echoed token: closing-quote-comma after dialogue before a speaker tag, parallel conjunctions/prepositions, repeated words, and URL/code/table delimiters (&, ?, |, http, —).

410m.description: Tokens that open or continue a modifier slot before an upcoming content word in a noun phrase or list: "non-", attributive "almost", "less" or "no", "and" between adjectives, first names, and "[@" after "and".
410m.explanation: Negation/degree modifiers (non, -, not, less, no, almost, unnecessarily) and coordinating 'and'/citation markers like '@' or '[@' right before an adjective or citation key, predicting the next word in a pair or list.

410m.description: Tokens right before a precise identifier, number or code that must come next: 'No.' in legal citations, form/route/date lead-ins, and repeated variable or symbol names in code and math.
410m.explanation: Predicts a repeated or structured identifier continuation: the token after 'No' (the period) in case/exhibit numbers, plus repeated variable/LaTeX pieces, hyphens in compound terms, and code identifier parts being copied.

410m.description: Mid-sentence clause-joining "but" after a concession, hedge or expectation ("I know this is stupid, but…", "originally planned…, but"). Weaker on code argument commas and minute digits in timestamps.
410m.explanation: The contrastive conjunction " but" following a comma after a concession or hedge clause ("I know this is stupid, but..."), anticipating a contrasting clause; weaker on commas and mid-word fragments.

410m.description: Relative pronouns (who/which/that) starting a clause that describes a preceding noun, strongest after 'and'/'or' ("and which"). Also 'and' continuing a modifier ("built in 1862 and"); weaker on boilerplate ("All rights reserved").
410m.explanation: Relative pronouns (that/which/who) introducing a relative clause, especially after a coordinating 'and'/'or'; also boilerplate continuations like 'All rights [reserved]', 'Local [Rule]', 'data' availability, and mid-word fragments.

410m.description: Linking token inside a fixed multi-word expression, especially the preposition in reduplicated idioms (side by side, time to time, one by one) and joiners in compounds (day-to-day, know-how).
410m.explanation: The connector token ("by", "to", "-", "of") inside a repeated or fixed idiom, predicting the repeated word, e.g. "side by side", "time to time", "day-to-day", "know-how", "out of", "all of a sudden".

410m.description: Polysemantic: commas/day/time tokens in travel-guide opening-hours lists (Mon-Sat[,]); kinship nouns after possessives (whose dad, mom, daughter-in-law); first count in subset breakdowns ((18 boys); plus miscellaneous tokens.
410m.explanation: Comma after 'Mon-Sat' in guidebook opening-hours listings, plus other mid-list or parenthetical tokens like numbers after '(' in statistics, 'dad'/'mom' possessives, and continuation points where a sequence will go on.

410m.description: Two jobs: (1) the preposition/'to' after a noun saying where it is or what's left to do ('X in mind', 'guns in hand', 'ales to sample'); (2) the letter after Mac/Mc in surnames (MacRinnalch, MacKenzie).
410m.explanation: Preposition/particle following a noun-object in an absolute-style phrase ("guns out", "goal in mind", "interest to uphold", "cash in his pocket"), plus the "R" in "MacRinnalch".

410m.description: Prose: the word after a subject saying what it causes or how good it is (made, resulting, giving, great, perfect). Separately, in math/code: absolute-value bars |, + operators, pipes.
410m.explanation: Predicts the next token after a subject/clause where a verb or connective of consequence/evaluation is expected (made, resulting, giving, seems, should, result); also fires on math/code delimiters like | and +\ inside formulas.

410m.description: Linking words inside set phrases of place, amount or naming, before the slot: 'miles north of', 'between', 'more than', '£X to £Y', 'known as', 'arm in arm', code 'return'.
410m.explanation: Function words completing a fixed phrase that expects a specific continuation: 'miles north [of]', 'halfway [between]', 'also known [as]', 'arm in [arm]', price ranges '£10 to £[25]', and 'return' statements in code.

410m.description: Mainly the second fragment of a word split after a short opening piece (R|ak, T|OU, M|rav, Dr|agg); also numbers after 'at least/more than/exactly', and commas closing opening if/when clauses.
410m.explanation: Mid-word subword fragments inside rare or multi-token words (TOURIST, Renovations, Draggables, Rakestraw), plus quantity words like 'one'/'1' after 'at least/exactly', and commas ending introductory clauses.

410m.description: Second/inner token completing a common fixed phrase or name, especially ' of' in 'Supreme Court of / State of / one of', plus 'for example', 'due (to)', 'in terms', 'console.log'.
410m.explanation: Connective function tokens that introduce a following noun phrase, mainly "of" after "one", "Supreme Court" or "population", plus "example"/"instance" in "for example", and "terms" and "due".

410m.description: Mostly prose words that open a clause or fixed phrase: sentence-initial "Never", "Ever", "There", "Nor", "Always", plus the first half of compounds like "there|between", "Life| Technologies" and "living| room". Weaker: dots and underscores inside identifiers in repeated code paths.
410m.explanation: Word/identifier joints where a compound is split mid-word or at a separator: 'there/here' before -between/-with/-of, 'Never' in 'never mind', and '.' or '_' in package/identifier names like org.apache.commons.math.dist.

410m.description: First token of a topic/domain-specific term or proper name (e.g. 'electric' cars, 'Mytilus', 'New' Zealand), strongly boosted when context already establishes or repeats that topic.
410m.explanation: Fires on the first token of a modifier or name (often a word fragment like 'My', 'New', 'D', 'electric') right after a determiner/preposition, where a specific noun (term, species, place, technology) is expected next.

410m.description: Mixed triggers: capital 'U' (U.S., Ugh), 'up to', 'in contrast', 'based', 'see/wonder what', 'people', citation/figure/version brackets, code dots, Q-title '?'. These often sit right before a predictable next word.
410m.explanation: Fires on a mid-phrase word or punctuation right after a preposition or clause start, where the next token is highly predictable: 'see [what]', 'in [contrast]', 'the [U].S.', 'at the [beginning]', 'things [people]', and '?' ending question titles.

410m.description: Polysemantic: sports win/loss counts ('won three straight games'), time-period nouns (week, weekend), legal citation names/judge titles (P.J., v. Sullivan), code methods (commit, group_by, join, end), stock phrases ('the end result', 'like many').
410m.explanation: Predicts a highly expected, formulaic continuation in fixed phrases or code: 'end result', 'straight games', 'week', 'All-', 'P.J.', 'group_by', 'end', where the next token is strongly predictable.

410m.description: Fires on slot-filling tokens in formulaic text: legal citations ("No.", volume numbers, "affixed"), polynomial variables, Wikipedia category "players", code indentation, and narrative "I almost"/"couldn't help but" or the subject right after a clause.
410m.explanation: Predicts a likely next token at mid-phrase function/structural positions: after 'almost' (laughed/smiled), 'No' in docket/case numbers, 'must', 'which', 'affixed', whitespace/newlines in code or legal text, and math-expression variables.

410m.description: Tokens inside long compound names written as one unit (run-together URLs, snake_case/ALL_CAPS code names, hyphenated chains like mother-in-law, all-caps titles); strongest on joining words like of/in/for/the.
410m.explanation: Mid-word or mid-compound fragments inside multi-word names glued together without spaces: URLs, all-caps identifiers, hyphenated phrases, and macro names, where a name or phrase is still continuing (e.g., www.white|horse, mother-in|-law).

410m.description: Mainly a subject pronoun after comparison/amount words ("than I", "as you", "the best I", "all we"); also name-fragment completions (Kluwer, Kettering), score digits (1-0), and variables in algebra drills.
410m.explanation: Predicts a pronoun or word completing a comparative or relative clause ("than [I]", "as [you]", "best [I] can"), plus predictable continuation tokens like Klu[wer], "1-[0]", and "if [it]".

2.8b.description: Word-internal subword fragments where the word continues (incomplete-word pieces), strongest for short v/r pieces like 'iv', 'av', 'ov', 'ir', 'vir' (conv-iv-ial, FEST-IV-AL); whole-word tokens don't fire.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-word subword fragments like "iv", "ir", "av", "ov" inside longer words (convivial, Oblivion, reactivate, captivating, festival), where the vowel+v/r piece sits in the middle of a word.

2.8b.description: Token completing a verb's object or complement, especially in set phrases and commands ("bear with me", "trust me", "forget X for", "look the other way"). Weak side pattern: code assignment '='.
2.8b.explanation: Token right after a verb/phrase where the object or completion is expected next, especially pronoun "me/them" after verbs like trust, bear with, listen to, stay with; also "=" in variable assignments in code.

2.8b.description: Nouns for an interaction or relation between two parties (X-to-X compounds, relationship, collaboration, match, coupling), and the verb after a subject naming an experiment or analysis in methods text.
2.8b.explanation: Fires on the word after a hyphen/compound or subject noun where a repeated or paired term is expected (e.g. one-on-[one], client-to-[client], Soviet [Union], 'processing [were]'), predicting the continuing word or verb.

2.8b.description: Tokens inside an unfinished clause or expression still awaiting its complement, strongest on verbs in 'to'-purpose phrases ("come … to see if"); also code openers like '([', '= ['.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts a continuation after a mid-phrase word, mostly transitive verbs or prepositions that await an object (admit, recognize, heard, account, to, for), plus opening brackets and colons introducing code or an example.

2.8b.description: Mid-clause tokens awaiting a complement: mainly transitive verbs after a subject or relative pronoun (owns, sells, provides, holds), speaker-named 'said/told', partitive 'of'/'own', and numbers in math/citations.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts a main verb or following word right after a subject noun/relative pronoun (e.g. 'that [owns/stores/provide]', 'Payton [said]', 'told'), plus mid-sequence tokens in lists and numbers; focuses on what comes next.

2.8b.description: Mainly words following death verbs in violent or mass-death contexts ("perished in", "killed in", "died during"); separately, weaker firing across code, math, legal and bibliographic citations, and archaic speech.
2.8b.explanation: Token right after a verb of dying/killing (died, killed, perished) predicting the next word, e.g. 'died [from/in/on/while]'; also fires on mid-word or next-token positions in prose and code.

2.8b.description: Mainly subword pieces from inside words ending in -s/-ps (catal|eps|y, B|ots|wana, rhod|ops|in). Separately: ' out' after movement verbs, and joining tokens in maths/code (LaTeX '}{\', ')*').
2.8b.explanation: Mid-word subword fragments, especially "eps", "ots", "ps", "ars", "aps" inside split words/names (Botswana, Cotswolds, dyspepsia, 'eps-matches'), plus "out" after verbs and LaTeX "{\" tokens.

2.8b.description: Fires on three unrelated things: variables in generated algebra expressions ("3*x**2"); dialogue reply openers or interjections (Yeah, Nope, Excuse, Japanese spoken lines); and phrases about needed fixes (require/need to/replacement/refurbishment).
2.8b.explanation: Fires on the token right after a start-of-utterance or mid-expression position: variable in math polynomial definitions (e.g. '*m**2'), first token of dialogue replies ('Yeah', 'Ex'cuse), Japanese subtitle starts, and verbs like 'require'.

2.8b.description: Text about costs, burdens or resource demands such as time, effort, money, space or energy being required, consumed, saved or reduced. Fires most strongly on 'required' or 'needed' after a resource noun (e.g. 'the long scan time required'), and weakly on obligations or drawbacks.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-clause tokens where the next word is a predicted continuation about a cost, burden, or requirement (e.g. reduce, required, more, space, have to), especially in problem/disadvantage contexts; also clause-boundary words and punctuation.

2.8b.description: Several unrelated triggers: the assignment `=` (and `:`/`||`) in code definitions; help-request verbs ("help", "suggest", "how"); the verb "watch"; methods words ("independently", "blind", "manually"); and miscellaneous word fragments or section numbers.
2.8b.explanation: Tokens right after a variable/property name that predict an upcoming value or object, mainly the assignment "=" in code (var x =), plus "help" in "can someone help me" and adverbs like "independently", "watch".

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: lone 'p' (or similar letter) fragments inside words or identifiers; words after hope, modals or imperatives (you, it, be); numbers and spacing in numeric tables and math; the word 'signed'.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-word or mid-structure tokens where the next piece is highly predictable continuation: split-word fragments (Her-p-az, out-p-acing), hyphens in names (HIM-6), numeric table cells and closing parentheses, and function words after verbs (do it, must be).

2.8b.description: Nouns/adverbs denoting an open-ended, varied set of multiple items: category plurals introducing examples ("artists like", "dishes such as"), list items, and distributive phrases ("every X", "here and there", "place to place").
2.8b.explanation: Plural category nouns (or list/index tokens) that head a set of examples, predicting a following "like/such as/including" or "here and there" enumeration, e.g. "TV shows like", "Famous students", "x_1".

2.8b.description: Mixed: effort/making idioms (from scratch, heavy lifting, real work), fragments inside unfamiliar names, hyphens in technical compounds (through-put), code tokens like ATOMIC, and role nouns like founder.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-word or mid-name fragments, especially after initials or in the middle of names and hyphenated compounds (D.P[.], Dan P[oul]ter, high through[-]put, USE_[AT]OMIC), where the next token is a continuation.

2.8b.description: Two related patterns: being new to or unfamiliar with something (new to, beginner, noob, unfamiliar, foreign, gain understanding), and the object/possessive after have/get/need (have your own car, get your bearings, meals).
2.8b.explanation: Word right after "I am/I'm/get/have/need" in phrases about a person's state or possessions, especially "I am [new] to..." (beginner/newbie) and "get/have [your/my/their] ..." (possessive pronoun), anticipating a noun or "to".

2.8b.description: Fires across text that argues, sells or makes claims (ads, advocacy, 'evidence proves', reported benefits or research results), peaking at commas, conjunctions, 'that' and claim verbs; near zero on neutral narrative or factual text.
2.8b.explanation: Syntactic junctures in expository prose where a clause or phrase continues: sentence-ending periods, commas, conjunctions (and/or/but), auxiliary verbs, and paragraph breaks, predicting what follows next, plus mid-word fragments.

2.8b.description: Tokens inside dense technical text (scientific papers, chemical names, statistics, code, logs and configs, legal or patent prose), especially in the middle of formulaic phrases; near zero on casual, narrative or everyday text.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-phrase function/connector tokens or separators (of, We, /, ,, -) where the next token is a continuation, often following numbers or digits like 5; common in scientific/chemical names and technical text.

2.8b.description: Strongest on boundary/range phrases: 'on the brink/verge/edge of', 'bordered on', 'fell within the range', 'falls into the category'. Separately fires on trailing numbers in synthetic algebra equations; scattered citation/code tokens.
2.8b.explanation: Tokens in the middle of a phrase where a predictable continuation follows: prepositions after 'fall/border/verge' (within, into, on), numbers within sequences, and words like 'as' before 'above' or 'is' predicting what comes next.

2.8b.description: The last token of a subject or left-hand operand, right before its predicate, value or relation. Strongest in a second, parallel or contrasting clause ("and women 30", "50% take"), closing math brackets and nested denominators.
2.8b.explanation: Tokens where the next word is highly predictable from structure: closing brackets/braces in LaTeX, repeated variables in algebra simplification, and unit nouns after 'per half/full' (day), or noun-phrase heads in set phrases.

2.8b.description: Fires on a fixed set of tokens, whether a whole word or part of one: bill/Bill, will/William, may/May, sam/Sam, count, king/King, can, shall. Unusual senses and names score higher; ordinary modal uses score lower.
2.8b.explanation: Word-start tokens like "Bill", "May", "Sam", "William", "count", "shall", "can" — especially the name Bill (also as fragment in billboard/billow/billings) — where the token could begin a longer word or be a name/word ambiguity.

2.8b.description: Words that close a phrase qualifying a quantity or extent ("or more", "if any", "not all", "in part", "very little"); weaker on fillers ("Um"), units after precise decimals and subject nouns in technical prose.
2.8b.explanation: Tokens ending a short phrase just before a likely closing/continuation, esp. parenthetical hedges like "if [any]", "in [part]", hesitation fillers (Um, Uh), and measurement unit tokens (mm, ppm) after numbers.

2.8b.description: Formal, technical or reference-style text: legal, contract and licence boilerplate, lab methods, citations, code/markup and LaTeX, IDs, chemical names, official-sounding dialogue. Near-silent on casual or simple narrative prose.
2.8b.explanation: Fires on highly predictable boilerplate/formulaic continuation tokens, where the next word is strongly determined: license text ('License for'), sentence-ending periods, mid-phrase words like 'Eagle', 'xsl:', 'Purch|aser', 'entit|les'.

2.8b.description: Mainly 'you' in 'Thank you' and other gratitude/apology/exclamation words (Thanks, Sorry, Oh my/Oh,). Separately: p<0.05 'indicated', scientific-notation exponent minus signs, and the 'made'/'Made' subword.
2.8b.explanation: Mainly the word "you" after "Thank" (also "Thanks" openers) in thank-you replies; weaker on "Oh,", statistical phrasing (p-value, indicated), and the hyphen in scientific notation like e-10.

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: code (`return -` before error codes, `+` in string concatenation, function-call parens), legal section citations, 'St' place names, set conversational phrases ('How are you', 'came to'), markdown/data line breaks.
2.8b.explanation: Predictable continuation tokens in structured text: the minus after 'return' in C error codes (-ENOMEM, -EINVAL), '=' or '+' operators after identifiers, list commas, 'you' after 'How are', and newline/indent tokens in repetitive lists.

2.8b.description: Tokens that point to a source or reference: attribution verbs ('As X writes/notes'), 'discussed in Section', citation keys/years, statute § numbers, closing quotes of cited phrases, URL paths.
2.8b.explanation: Citation/attribution and cross-reference slots: the word right after "As [Author]" (writes, notes, explains, words), "discussed/described [in/below]", or inside citation numbers and closing quotes, where a source or referenced passage comes next.

2.8b.description: Partitive quantity constructions: fires on 'of' and the following determiner in 'some/most/many/much/a lot/majority/half of (the/my/them)', strongest for 'some of' and 'a lot of the'.
2.8b.explanation: The word right after a partitive quantifier like "some", "much", "most", "a lot", or "majority", especially the "of" or "the" in "some of the…" / "most of the…", predicting a following noun phrase.

2.8b.description: Final subword tokens of multi-token proper names, especially Pokémon or athletes in lists. Also: specific-recall slots like computed arithmetic-answer digits, speech verbs before character names, 'mutations' in genomic records.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts the next token in rigidly patterned or structured text: mid-word fragments of names, the 'mutations=' field in cigar strings, dialogue speech verbs after quotes (pleaded, sighed), LaTeX/code continuations and number digits.

2.8b.description: Token just before an expected ordinal or count word, strongest at 'the'/'for'/'is' in novelty claims like 'this is [the] first study', 'for [the] first time'; weaker for other counts or numbers.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts upcoming "first"/"only"/ordinal words: fires on determiners or prepositions in phrases like "this is [the] first study", "for [the] first time", "not [the] first time", "between [any] two", "all [but] one".

2.8b.description: Clause boundaries in explanatory/guidebook prose: sentence-final periods, ')' or ';' closing a remark; predicate verbs after a subject (caught, stuck, lodged, found); conditionals (if, unless). Plus scattered code word-pieces.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-sentence tokens where a clause could end or continue: sentence-final periods/closing parens after a complete statement, plus verbs/connectives (put, lodged, found, introduce) predicting the next word. Also mid-word fragments like 'oc'.

2.8b.description: Several unrelated jobs. Strongest: subject pronoun after a knowing/uncertainty verb ("knew I", "not sure what we") and mid-word chunks of rare/scientific names (Am-arant-e). Weaker: repeated code, citation and math syntax.
2.8b.explanation: Tokens in the middle of a word or structure where the next token is a predictable continuation: subject pronouns after 'what/if/whether/knew' (I, he), mid-word fragments of rare names, and code/LaTeX delimiters like ';' or ','.

2.8b.description: Text about where money or resources go: funding, proceeds, spending, or allocating, splitting, spreading or redirecting them. Strongest on the word that sets the destination ('go to', 'will', 'redistributed', 'funded by').
2.8b.explanation: Verbs/words about funding, paying, or allocating money/resources (funded, financed, split, spread, allocated, distributed, diverted, proceeds will), especially predicting the next word like 'by', 'to', or the money recipient/purpose.

2.8b.description: Formulaic math-problem text (factor/divide questions, n'th term, nested arithmetic/sqrt expressions) and repetitive structured code/citations; also oddly fires on name subwords like Mahathir's "ath" and Calhoun's "h".
2.8b.explanation: Predicts the next token in synthetic math-problem and structured code text: the number after "Is/Does" in divisibility questions, the "h" of "i'th term", closing parentheses in function definitions, and tabs or newlines in repetitive lists.

2.8b.description: Talk of quantities that flow, change or are compared: input/output, production/consumption, intake/release, amounts, or 'more X than Y'. Fires hardest on the hinge token ('and', 'than we', 'it is') joining the paired flows.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens in paired or comparative constructions (X and/or Y, input/output, more than, much more than we), where the next word must mirror an earlier term (e.g., 'and' joining parallel nouns, 'than we export').

2.8b.description: Expressions of desire for a different or better state than the current one: wishing (esp. pronoun after 'wish'), regret, counterfactuals, needs, improvements, alternatives, and complaints implying something should change.
2.8b.explanation: Token right after a wish/desire/need construction, predicting a hypothetical or desired clause: mainly the subject after "wish" ("I wish [I]"), also "need [for]", "call [for]", "better [way]", "there had to [be]".

2.8b.description: Fires on the token right before an expected pronoun (it/them/they) referring back to an earlier noun, e.g. 'feel to| it', 'in that| it', 'brought with| them', 'wasn't| it'.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts an upcoming pronoun (it/them/they) referring back to a just-mentioned subject; fires on prepositions, 'that', 'because', or punctuation right before the pronoun, e.g. 'has a nice heft to [it]', 'in that [it]', 'brought with [it]'.

2.8b.description: Dense technical/legal/scientific text and code: peaks on role 'as', sentence-opening linkers (As, In addition), commas in legal lists, and line breaks inside nested code blocks.
2.8b.explanation: Function-word or structural tokens at a boundary where a continuation is expected: sentence-initial "As" and "as" after verbs like 'used'/'acts', plus newlines after closing braces in code and XSL 'otherwise' tags.

2.8b.description: Expressions of degree or extent: 'so X (that)', 'so much so', 'to the point/extent that', 'as high/low as', 'enough', and range endpoints 'from X to Y', 'until'.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-construction tokens in degree/extent or range phrases where a continuation is expected: the "so [much/good/big]" before "that/so", "to the point/extent", and range connectors like "from X [to] Y", "as low as".

2.8b.description: Connector or continuation tokens inside multi-part names and compounds. Strongest on a hyphen after a proper noun or acronym ("Seattle-based", "US-China"), and on name pieces, name possessives and "P.3d"-type citations. Weaker on dialogue-boundary quotes and code type arguments.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-word or mid-compound continuation tokens: suffixes, hyphens, possessive 's, or fragments of names and citations (e.g. Bank-Illinois, cousin's, P.3d), where the next token continues an ongoing multi-part name or phrase.

2.8b.description: A broad context or register unit: it fires on mid-phrase tokens in dense, formal or technical text (science, encyclopedia, legal, math, code). It stays near zero in casual, chatty or simple narrative prose.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-expression tokens in math/code/technical text where the next token is a predictable continuation: LaTeX braces after \frac, operators, brackets, numbers, or nouns like 'system', 'samples', 'of'.

2.8b.description: Forward-looking or uncertain statements about what will or might happen: modals (will, may, could), hedges (likely, doubtless, expect), conditionals, and travel-guide practical info (prices 'from £', nearest station).
2.8b.explanation: Function words or modal/auxiliary tokens right after a subject or noun phrase, where a predicate or verb phrase is expected next (e.g. 'will', 'should', 'be', 'might', 'of', 'doubt[less]'), predicting what follows.

2.8b.description: Strongest on US case-law citations (pin-cite page numbers, page-range ends, the ')' closing a court/year). Weaker on words continuing parallel or set phrases ('Society of', 'times more likely', 'main difference', 'uses as well').
2.8b.explanation: Legal citation internals: closing parenthesis after a year, or final digits of page/pin-cite numbers in case reporters (F.2d, U.S., P.2d); also weakly digits in math strings and mid-phrase function words.

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: fires in PHP code (newlines, indents, $_POST), plot summaries ('tells the story of'), long number/index/patent lists, legal opinions, travel-guide hours, and odd word fragments (succ-um-bed, Thess-al-onica).
2.8b.explanation: Predicts continuation of structured or repetitive sequences: list separators in index/number lists, blank-line or indentation tokens in PHP code, and mid-word fragments (succ-um-bed, Thess-al-onica); fires on the delimiter or fragment token.

2.8b.description: Fires where a text announces or anticipates an authoritative decision or required action on something, e.g. 'must/should be [dismissed/reversed/removed]', 'Accordingly,', 'motion is', strongest in court rulings.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts the verb or auxiliary after a subject in legal/judicial or directive statements ("must", "should", "will", "be"), e.g. "judgment must be reversed", and the comma after "Accordingly" in court rulings.

2.8b.description: Nouns naming an industry, sector or field (music, law, security, software, energy, gas, app) used as the modifier in a compound, plus hyphens after such nouns (book-, gun-); also abbreviations in company/statute names.
2.8b.explanation: Industry/domain noun or hyphen/abbreviation used as the first element of a compound or noun phrase (music, game, law, security, energy, app, book-, Elec.) where the next token continues the compound, e.g. 'music business', 'law enforcement'.

2.8b.description: Wistful prose/poetry about time passing, loss, fading or distance ("days fly by", "far away", stanza breaks in elegiac poems); separately, code string escapes ("\n", "\t") and flag literals like "= 1".
2.8b.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens where the next word is highly predictable: idiomatic distance/time phrases (not too far [off], days fly [by], far [away]), blank-line breaks in poems/lyrics, and code format-string or literal tokens like ("\ and 1.

2.8b.description: Tokens that set up an upcoming quantity or magnitude: change or comparison words ('by', 'at', 'or' in 'less than or equal'), measure nouns ('distance', 'height'), and code assignments or arguments before numbers.
2.8b.explanation: Tokens right before a numeric value or quantity is stated, especially after a change/comparison verb (increased by, at least, on the order of, to a lesser extent, equal to), or an assignment/colon before a value.

2.8b.description: Instrumental/means constructions: fires on use/using/used/with (instrumental) and especially the following determiner/possessive/modifier introducing the tool or means used for an action; weaker on tool nouns themselves.
2.8b.explanation: Tokens right after an instrumental 'with'/'using'/'use' that introduce the tool or means of an action (e.g. 'with [his] finger', 'using [a]', 'used [the]'), predicting the instrument noun next.

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: legal opinions/case citations (in/quoting before case names, court phrasing), titles before politicians' names, 'how/the way/the more you' clauses, plus scattered code identifiers and paragraph breaks.
2.8b.explanation: Function words or punctuation at mid-sentence points where a continuation is highly predictable (e.g., 'in' before a case name, 'the' in 'the X-er the Y-er', legal citations, paragraph-break newlines); a syntactic-slot predictor, most common in legal text.

2.8b.description: Fires where the next token is expected to be arbitrary and hard to predict: inside IDs, long numbers, citation keys, hashes, table rulers, and before varied lists ("a diverse group/eclectic mix of").
2.8b.explanation: Mid-token fragments in structured or scraped text: markdown table separator dashes, citation/reference IDs (e.g. @gks1234-B, 1471-2164-14-505), figure filenames, and numeric delimiters; also occasionally 'diverse' or 's.

2.8b.description: Non-passive ' by' (by-product, byword, by now, by email, by name); verbs for getting information after 'to' (receive, read, request, learn); first pieces of split words (head|way, sta|unch).
2.8b.explanation: Fires mid-phrase on the word "by" (also "read", "receive", "request") where a fixed idiom or compound is expected, e.g. "by-product", "by reputation", "day by day", and on standalone numbers/line breaks.

2.8b.description: Mid-phrase tokens in conventional fixed expressions: legal reporter dots (F.2d after case names), 'et al.'/'&'/'and' joining names, unit exponents (L^−1), and abundance phrases ('wide variety/range of', 'everything').
2.8b.explanation: Predicts the next token in a highly formulaic citation or notation pattern: the period in legal reporter cites like 'F.2d', 'et' before 'al.', '&' in names, exponent digits like '^−1^'; also some filler words.

2.8b.description: Polysemantic. Strongest on operands and closing parentheses deep inside synthetic arithmetic/algebra expressions ("Let a be 7 + (-7 - -7)"). Also fires on stock phrases ("to the best of our"), code-structure tokens and assorted mid-sentence prose tokens.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-expression tokens where the next token is highly predictable from a pattern: operands/variables in synthetic algebra and arithmetic problems (numbers, x, n, closing parens), plus completions of multi-token names or phrases.

2.8b.description: Separator token (–, -, and, or, &, comma, column gap) between parallel items in ranges, paired opposite terms or structured lists (weekdays, page ranges, elements, symmetric/antisymmetric), where the next item is predictable.
2.8b.explanation: Connector tokens inside lists or ranges (hyphen/en dash in day or page ranges like Sun-Thu or 261–266, commas in index page lists, 'and'/'&' joining paired items), where the next item is expected to follow.

2.8b.description: Mainly middle pieces of words split into several tokens (rare names like Kochenberger, Gauguin; code constants like DB_VERIFY_BAD). Also polite refusals ('No thanks,'), newlines after photo credits, and 'the court' before rulings.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-word fragments of rare names/technical terms (K-oc-henberger, Gaug-uin), plus 'the court' subject tokens in legal text, and newline after image captions/credits; predicts a continuation token.

2.8b.description: Mixed unit: mid-phrase tokens in disclaimer/web boilerplate and some stock phrases ("none of your business", "sole responsibility"), plus unrelated code indentation/braces, math operators, wiki "Category:" colons and dialogue quote marks.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-phrase function words/punctuation in stock or idiomatic expressions where a specific continuation is highly predictable (e.g., 'none of your business', 'opinions expressed... sole responsibility', 'make sure', 'please see', 'use the').

2.8b.description: Mainly sentence-initial discourse connectives and reply words (However, Therefore, Conversely, Yes, Yeah, Why) starting a new sentence or reply; also code and math break points (shell then/do, braces, fraction slashes).
2.8b.explanation: Sentence-start connectives and function words that predict a continuation, like "Therefore", "Conversely", "However", "Yeah"/"Yes" answers, and "the"/"why", plus syntax tokens in code and LaTeX.

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: footnote 'n.' in legal citations; partitive 'of' (one of/last of); comparative 'like'; code member-access dots; arithmetic operators in math problems; LaTeX '='; semicolons; mid-word name/compound pieces.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-token predicting a continuation after an abbreviation/partial word: mostly the period in legal footnote citations ("n." before a number), plus "like"/"of" and word-fragment tokens in the middle of compounds.

2.8b.description: Fires where text is about to name an item set up by context: one of two after 'two'/'both', math subscripts and index pairs, subjects after inverted place phrases ('next to X is the…'), earlier-defined terms.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts the next token in contexts where a pair/duality was set up (two, both, one of, first of two) or a subscript index follows; fires on structural tokens like underscores, commas, 'is', 'the' before the second element.

2.8b.description: Several unrelated triggers: newline ending a short mid-document heading; analysis verbs (analyse, analyzing, examine); scenic travel-guide description (waves lap, lush green); HTML/XML/PHP markup tokens (=", <, >, (').
2.8b.explanation: Newline/blank-line tokens after short heading or title lines (section headers in scraped web text), plus the word 'analy-' forms (analyse, analytical) and scattered tokens in code or citations.

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: fires on pet names (sweet/sweetie/love), quantity words after feel/spend (some, any, a little), set-phrase words (enough to, buried in), the slash in 'x**9/504', and random ID strings.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-word fragments and quantifier/preposition tokens after verbs of feeling, plus affectionate 'sweet'/'love' terms (sweetie, Luv) and random-string/ID pieces; fires where a following noun or word continuation is expected.

2.8b.description: Verbs and prepositions placing an entity at, or moving it through/to/past, a place, e.g. 'buses stop in X', 'line passes through', 'located in', 'lived here', 'ingrowth into'.
2.8b.explanation: Verbs or prepositions right after a subject, predicting a location/path complement: especially buses/lines 'stop', 'pass', 'come' through/in a place (travel-guide transit phrasing), and motion/position words before 'to/in/at/through'.

2.8b.description: Tokens inside highly conventional, templated text such as legal reporter citations, lab-method units and reagents, boilerplate disclaimers, and code or markup syntax (attribute =", brackets, newlines). Weak on casual prose.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts the next token at highly formulaic mid-pattern positions in structured text: code/markup syntax (type=", <, =>), legal citation numbers (S.Ct. 72), and scientific units/concentrations (0.01 M, toluene).

2.8b.description: Two unrelated jobs: words leading into a novelty or ordinal claim ("this is [the] first…", "for [the] first time", "only the fifth"), and a word-initial capital "E" token (EDS, E-cadherin, Este, variable E).
2.8b.explanation: Tokens right before "first" in "for the first time" / "this is the first study/report" novelty claims (mostly "the", "for", "reported"); also a weaker firing on capital "E" starting names or acronyms.

2.8b.description: Several unrelated triggers: 'pone'/'ppat' in PLOS figure links ("](#pone."), repeated numbers in sqrt arithmetic, '95% CI', 'Pacific'/'Atlantic', fluorophore/reagent terms, '__be32', and 'I' in embedded or question clauses.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts a repeated or highly predictable continuation token: copying an identifier from earlier context (e.g. 'pone' in PLOS ONE refs, '475' in ISSN, repeated numbers) or a common next word (I, just, CI, Pacific).

2.8b.description: Mostly past participles after a noun or as header labels ("powder made from", "table constructed", "Edited by", "updated"). Also clause openers: if/whether/what/that, sentence-start "That's why", "You".
2.8b.explanation: Mid-sentence word right after a noun or verb phrase that expects a continuation, often a participle, preposition, or complementizer (made, derived, constructed, if, that, of, want), anticipating what follows. Also 'previous/above [Lemma/theorem]'.

2.8b.description: Nouns or variables naming a quantity whose value is being specified (energy, concentration, altitude, √s, f, ℓ) and, relatedly, capacity nouns (ability, competency, capability, condition) before 'to'.
2.8b.explanation: Fires on the head token of a physical quantity or variable (T, s, r, f, energy, frequency, sensitivity, ability) in scientific/LaTeX text, where a threshold, range, or inequality or 'of/to' complement is expected next.

2.8b.description: Mixed unit: causal verbs taking an object (inspired, led, allowed, motivated, drove, spurred, prevent); fixed phrases (bursting at the seams, beyond reasonable doubt, at this point); code 'public'; numbered bus routes in travel guides.
2.8b.explanation: Fires on a word in a highly predictable fixed phrase or idiom, where the token continues a collocation (e.g. 'beyond a reasonable doubt', 'bursting at the seams', 'inspired', 'Bus 118' in transit listings).

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: digits inside number-sequence terms; first word of a dialogue reply after a question; comparison/limit words (far, at most/least, only, all very well); '&' in business names.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens where the next word is a predictable completion: quantifier/comparative idioms (at most/least, far exceed, fine), opening quotes in dialogue, digits in arithmetic sequences, and ampersand/'and' in names.

2.8b.description: Free-choice "any" after verbs/prepositions (outweighs any, thanks for any, than any); comparison/override words (than, beat, supersede); connectors to the next number in ranges/lists ("4GB to 8GB", "or even").
2.8b.explanation: Predicts a following quantity/object after a transitive verb or connector: 'any' after verbs/prepositions (met any burden, REPLACE any), and 'to/and/than/,' in numeric ranges or comparisons (4GB to 8GB, 25 and 35).

2.8b.description: Fires where items of an announced set or list are about to begin: the boundary after "There are two reasons for this.", list markers like (ii) or (4), and "one of" or "most of" a group.
2.8b.explanation: Punctuation or list markers right after an announced enumeration ("two reasons/options/methods"), predicting the items to follow: the period/colon ending the intro sentence, or "(ii)", "one [of]", "most" in list enumerations.

2.8b.description: Tokens inside an unfinished multi-token unit: pieces of rare/foreign words, pronunciation respellings, hyphen/dot joins in compounds and identifiers, and words partway through set phrases (out of, by any).
2.8b.explanation: Mid-word or mid-compound continuation tokens (hyphens, syllable fragments, punctuation, function words) where the next piece is a predictable continuation, e.g. pronunciation guides, name fragments, identifiers, LaTeX/code separators, and phrasal 'of/or/to'.

2.8b.description: Mainly tokens in generated polynomial math problems, especially '**' exponents (e.g. 'Let f(x) = -x**3 + 16*x**2'); also MDPI anchor volume numbers ('behavsci-10-'), and scattered unrelated prose/code tokens.
2.8b.explanation: The exponent operator "**" in polynomial expressions of synthetic math problems (e.g. "Let f(x) be the derivative of x**4/4 + 10*x**3/3"); weaker on mid-word/compound continuation tokens like gamma-ray, Zariski, and "10" in IDs.

2.8b.description: Mid-token positions in dense technical notation: email username starts ("Email: dr"), coefficient '*' in algebra drills, decimals in stats tables or intervals, LaTeX/markup tokens; weaker diffuse firing in formal prose.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-token positions where the next token is highly predictable continuation: operators/digits in algebra exercises (e.g., '2[[*]]c**2'), decimals in stats tables, LaTeX fragments, split words/emails (inter|pelado, dr.), and prepositions in fixed phrases.

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: fires most on obsessive/compulsive/fanatical words; also on time-span words and season or category years, sports 'within N points', and pieces inside rare proper names.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-word or mid-phrase tokens predicting a continuation: especially "obsess(ive)", "adren(aline)", year/time expressions ("-" in 2014-15, "years", "decade", "year"), category year labels ("Category:1978"), and name fragments.

2.8b.description: Tokens inside fixed, formulaic multi-token sequences that strongly determine what follows: citation volume numbers, day numbers after months, set phrases (here and now, Look out), code assignments and identifier pieces.
2.8b.explanation: Predictive mid-pattern tokens in formulaic text: legal citations (reporter volume numbers, commas after case names), date day-numbers after month, assignment operators in code, and mid-word fragments, where the next token is highly predictable.

2.8b.description: Tokens inside fixed multi-token sequences: license/legal/web boilerplate (e.g. '(at your option)'), compound code identifiers, set phrases like '2020 season', and names split into word pieces.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts a highly formulaic continuation token inside boilerplate or multi-token identifiers, e.g. "(at) your option" in GPL text, "call-template", "Return to text", and mid-word or underscore pieces.

2.8b.description: Fires right before a boolean value in code (`x =`, `return`, `flag:` before true/false), and in prose that lists alternatives or variants ("there are two forms/varieties", "at least", "yes vs. no").
2.8b.explanation: Predicts an upcoming boolean/enumerated value or count: fires on assignment operators before true/false (flag = true), and on 'There are two/at least' phrases introducing forms, varieties or species.

2.8b.description: Mid-word subword fragments that need a continuation, strongest right after a word-initial 'F'/'f' (F[av]re, F[ais]al, f[ath]oming, F[fest]iniog); weaker on stems like ' suffer', ' lag', ' dwell'.
2.8b.explanation: Word-continuation tokens after an initial 'F'/'f' fragment, where a word or name starting with F is split into subword pieces (e.g. F|ais|al, F|fest|iniog, F|ult|on, f|ath|oming); also nearby 'fail/free/full'.

2.8b.description: Words that fill out a predictable verb construction or idiom: purpose infinitives ('to dry', 'to choose from'), particles ('sat down', 'ran out'), reflexives, 'to which [subject]'. Scattered code/math tokens too.
2.8b.explanation: Fires on the word after an infinitive 'to' or a 'to which' construction, where a verb or complement of a stranded/fronted clause is expected (e.g. 'to dry', 'introduce themselves', 'enough to'); also some code and LaTeX tokens.

2.8b.description: Fires on the word-start fragment token "Se"/"se"/"SE" when it begins a word split into pieces (Seçmen, Señor, seine, Severe). Weaker: other capital fragments like He, E, Y.
2.8b.explanation: Fires on the word-start fragment " Se"/"SE" (also "E", "HE", "Y") as a token beginning a word or name, e.g. Seçmen, Señorías, Seahawks, SECONDS; strongest after "Toplam" in Turkish election tables.

2.8b.description: Mid-phrase tokens in fluent, conventional text or code where a familiar construction is under way: main verbs after modals, 'to' or adverbs; participles in route descriptions; member-access dots and hex '0'.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts the next token mid-phrase at a point where a continuation is expected: verbs/function words after a subject or auxiliary in legal prose, '.' before method names (System.out.), and '0' before 'x' in hex constants.

2.8b.description: Left-hand operand of a test in a conditional (if/while/assert before ==, <, !=), strongest on the token just before the operator; weaker on prose 'if/when X is' clauses and comparisons.
2.8b.explanation: Tokens inside a conditional or comparison expression just before the comparison/predicate continues (e.g. `if (j <`, `x ===`, `& 0x7) !=`, `if forgn is`), mostly in code, plus similar mid-clause positions in prose.

2.8b.description: Two related patterns of comparison against a reference: lists of change verbs and phrases stating a difference ('add, remove, or', 'the only difference is'), and limit or expectation phrases ('as far as it would go', 'not that hard').
2.8b.explanation: Predicts a continuation after a coordinated list item or comparative clause: commas/"and"/"or" in lists of verbs or adjectives, and auxiliaries/predicates after "as ... as they/it" or "the only difference" constructions.

2.8b.description: Tokens inside an unfinished unit whose continuation is tightly constrained: fragments of rare or long words, function words partway through set phrases, open math brackets, decimal points.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-word subword fragments or mid-expression tokens where the continuation is highly predictable: split rare words (irrep-ress-ible, e-leg-ans, anach-ronism), LaTeX/number syntax pieces, and "even/to/as" in fixed phrases.

2.8b.description: Fires on 'life/lives' as an entity whose course or fate is described (esp. as subject: 'his life was…', 'life has been'), and following verb tokens; weaker for analogous spans (career, reign, game).
2.8b.explanation: Predicts what follows the word "life" (or similar subjects like career, reign) — fires on "life" itself and on the next token ("was", "has"), especially in phrases like "his life was in danger", "life-threatening", and "ground to a halt".

2.8b.description: Tokens inside fixed multi-token units: mid-word name pieces, citation page numbers and footnote markers, line breaks before reference headings, code syntax (<?php, return;), compounds and stock phrases.
2.8b.explanation: Fires on structural/formatting tokens in the middle of a pattern: blank lines before section headings (External links, References), citation page-range digits, footnote markers like [^], hyphens in citation syntax, and mid-word fragments.

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: 'so' in 'and so on/forth'; 'spread' meaning layout; 'along' in 'along with'; first pieces of split words (Fer-ries, St-ain-less, Sp-it, Emb-ryonic); weaker on 'need' and code delimiters.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-phrase function words or word fragments where the next token is a highly predictable continuation, especially "and [so] on/forth", plus subword pieces (Sp-, Fer-, Emb-) and connectors like "of", "need", "why".

2.8b.description: Tokens inside fixed multi-token units: mainly 'in' adverbial phrases ('In any case/event', 'in winter/October', 'in the future'), plus internal pieces of proper names (Sar-ap-en, Washington Post, W1).
2.8b.explanation: Word right after a sentence-initial "In" in fixed phrases ("In any case/event", "In other words", "In the..."), also "in" before seasons/months; weaker on mid-name tokens like Sar-ap-en, S-amp-els.

2.8b.description: Fires on words inside clauses about a needed, wanted or possible outcome ("tools that work", "so that", "as much as possible", "requires that X be deposited"), but not on plain past facts. Also fires at sentence or entry boundaries: final periods, newlines, opening brackets.
2.8b.explanation: Sentence-ending newlines/periods (end of a sentence or paragraph, before a new line), plus mid-sentence positions after an adverb/adjective or verb where a complement is expected (e.g. 'sufficiently', 'accurately').

2.8b.description: Mainly distance and location phrases in travel-guide listings ("a mile south of", "10 minutes' walk", venue nouns, end-of-entry periods); also unrelated hex literals, court signature blocks, function-call brackets in math problems, and code tokens.
2.8b.explanation: Tokens completing a distance/time expression in travel-guide directions ("half a mile", "10 minutes' walk", "1.5 miles east"), plus similar predictable continuation tokens like "Circuit Judge" and math/code syntax.

2.8b.description: Strongest on hyphens and range words ("6-month", "six- and eight-", "four to six") and on study-design phrasing ("This study was", "followed for", "Short Form"). Weaker on code identifiers and formula punctuation.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens in scientific/technical text where a predictable continuation follows: hyphens after durations (6-month, 24-hour), 'This' opening study descriptions, 'Short' in medical names, and split code identifiers (CreatePreparer).

2.8b.description: Tokens completing a predictable stock construction in technical, code, markup or boilerplate text: figure/table number refs, share-widget line breaks, code syntax, set phrases and terms. Stronger with longer context; near zero in casual prose.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts the next structural token in scientific/web boilerplate, especially the number inside table/figure reference links like "(Table [3](#Tab3){ref-type", plus newlines after share/like lines and mid-phrase tokens.

2.8b.description: Section-opening headings or transition phrases in formal legal, scientific and mathematical text (Analysis, CONCLUSION, Proof, Introduction, 'Upon review', 'the following'), plus the later piece of some fixed compound terms (401(k), hyperactivity, anger-management).
2.8b.explanation: Section-heading and formal-document structure tokens in legal/scientific text (ANALYSIS, CONCLUSION, Proof, 'Upon review/consideration', 'following'), where the next token is a newline or the section body begins.

2.8b.description: Two related framing roles: interjections/discourse markers (uh-huh hyphen, oh, ahh, hmm, okay) and abstract/general category nouns that classify a referent appositively or predicatively ("an event that", "a right we", "is an art").
2.8b.explanation: Interjections like "Ah/Oh/Uh/Hmm" (often elongated, e.g. "Uh-huh", "Ahh") starting an utterance, and the noun right after the indefinite article "a" in appositive descriptions ("a peninsula", "a genus").

2.8b.description: Wh-words (why/what/who) opening direct or rhetorical questions in dialogue; continuation points in parallel lists ('two or three', repeated 'Model'/'class', '(c)'); and the 'ib' token in Halliburton/halibut.
2.8b.explanation: Predicts a continuation in an enumerated or parallel series: sentence-initial rhetorical "Why" after a comma/period, list markers like " (" before iv/C, numbered line starts, "Hall-ib-urton" fragments, and repeated sequence/citation tokens.

2.8b.description: Polysemantic. Fires on code getters/accessors (get, getX, @return, pointer *), '=' in math definitions, table separator columns, prose determiners after prepositions (this/each/both), and words partway through fixed phrases (knocked/banging on).
2.8b.explanation: Mid-construct tokens where the next token is a predictable continuation: code identifiers (get/return/current), operators like '=' or '*', whitespace padding in tables, and idiom words (a kick, both times).

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: closing punctuation of quoted dialogue; 'report(s)'; 'own' after possessives; verbs in 'who' clauses ('who has to', 'who'll get'); inner subword pieces of names/chemicals/code identifiers.
2.8b.explanation: Fires at points where the next token is a predictable continuation: mid-word fragments of names and identifiers (Goebbels, Analyzer), sentence-final punctuation after 'he said', and words like 'own', 'only', 'who'.

2.8b.description: Words for response, causation and timing (delayed, leading, driving, response, reactive, active, sensitive, signal, trigger, blocking, slow), strongest before a noun. The abbreviation 'PE' also fires strongly.
2.8b.explanation: Word pieces like lead/leading, delay(ed), active/reactive/responsive, response, driving, sensitive, PE, send/transmit: dynamic process or causation words, often as the first part of a compound or modifier before a noun.

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: directional particles (back, behind, over, inside, off); 'What is/would be' in Q&A questions; linking words (both, either, and, of) in academic prose; code newlines and hex digits; name fragments.
2.8b.explanation: Mid-phrase function/connector tokens that expect a continuation: prepositions/particles after verbs (back, behind, inside, over, off), 'of' after 'one', 'and', plus newlines after code closing braces and colons or hex digits in code.

2.8b.description: Tokens opening or premodifying an argument/noun-phrase slot before its head: determiners/adjectives after verbs/prepositions ('write a', 'a wide'); in code, types, constructors, function/macro names after :, :=, ., =.
2.8b.explanation: Fires on a token in the middle of a construct where a specific kind of continuation is strongly expected: articles/adjectives before a noun ("a", "an", "all"), or code syntax like ":", ":=", "!", "join", "define" before a type or argument.

2.8b.description: Polysemantic: seek/sought/trying/looking-to/wanted verbs; exclamative 'such (a)'; LaTeX exponent/subscript markers (^, _, ^{) as in χ^2; word-piece after an initial capital in rare proper nouns (A|eg|ibong, A|ired|ales).
2.8b.explanation: Tokens that begin a short fragment where the next token is highly predictable: exponent carets (^) in LaTeX math like χ^2, the verb 'seek/sought', 'Such a', and mid-word pieces or long whitespace-indentation in code.
